items.descriptionOriginal: Spacecraft could soon share a common refueling connection, potentially changing how operators manage satellites in orbit. Spaceium has released OpenPort, an open-source interface that any company can license and manufacture for just $1. The design lets spacecraft receive fuel after launch instead of relying entirely on their onboard reserves. It will also undergo an orbital demonstration aboard the International Space Station. Common refueling standard Most satellites carry a fixed supply of propellant for their planned missions. Once that supply runs low, operators often retire otherwise functional spacecraft. Their electronics and other systems might remain operational, but limited fuel can end their usefulness. A lack of standardized connections has also complicated orbital refueling efforts. Different manufacturers develop their own interfaces, forcing operators to consider compatibility before arranging fuel transfers. A tanker built by one company might not connect with another manufacturer’s spacecraft. OpenPort aims to address that problem through an identical connection on both spacecraft. Its androgynous design allows either vehicle to supply or receive propellant. That means a satellite could potentially refuel another spacecraft instead of relying exclusively on dedicated tankers. The interface also replaces a conventional fill-and-drain valve. Those connections typically serve ground fueling operations before launch. OpenPort keeps the connection functional after a spacecraft reaches orbit. Spaceium says its design handles higher pressures and greater docking misalignment than competing refueling interfaces. These capabilities could help spacecraft establish reliable connections during demanding orbital operations. Xenon transfer reaches orbit OpenPort’s upcoming demonstration will take place aboard the International Space Station. Spaceium plans to fly the hardware as a NASA-approved external payload through Voyager Technologies’ commercial payload service. During the demonstration, the interface will transfer xenon between two tanks in orbit. Spaceium describes this as the first-ever xenon transfer performed in orbit. The mission will test whether spacecraft can exchange propellant through a standardized connection. The demonstration follows another Spaceium mission in February 2026. Its precision robotic actuator successfully completed its first space mission after launching aboard a SpaceX rideshare. Building a refueling network Spaceium wants OpenPort to become a widely adopted connection across the spacecraft industry. Its broader business model centers on automated orbital stations that sell propellant as a service. Co-founder and CEO Ashi Dissanayake says the company sees the stations as its primary business. Every spacecraft equipped with OpenPort could eventually become a potential customer. “The port isn’t the business. The stations are,” Dissanayake said . He believes widespread adoption will create demand for orbital refueling services, including those operated by competitors. Founded by aerospace and mechanical engineers Dissanayake and Reza Fetanat, Spaceium joined Y Combinator’s Summer 2024 batch. Its commercial customers include operators pursuing orbital transfer vehicles, lunar missions and geostationary satellites. The company plans to establish refueling stations across low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit. Its longer-term ambitions also include stations along routes to the Moon. A common connection could eventually help satellite operators extend spacecraft lifespans. It could also allow lunar missions and orbital transfer vehicles to travel farther without carrying all their propellant from Earth. Spaceium is expanding its engineering team as it prepares for the ISS demonstration and its first refueling station. OpenPort’s adoption will ultimately determine whether different spacecraft manufacturers embrace a shared standard.

Now, a landmark phase 3 clinical trial of a personalized melanoma vaccine shows that this approach can improve outcomes for patients. Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center was among the clinical centers that participated in the multicenter study.

Πέρασε περίπου μισή ώρα σε κάθε στάση δ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Mechanical loading is important for maintaining bone mass, and researchers from Science Tokyo have found that sensory nerves inside the bone play a key role in this process. In mice, sensory nerve abundance changed in response to mechanical unloading and reloading, and removing these nerves prevented bone recovery. The findings reveal a link between mechanical loading, sensory nerves and bone recovery and could support sensory nerve-targeted therapies and rehabilitation strategies for osteoporosis and fragility.

Η Microsoft πιστεύει πλέον ότι συνέβαλαν οι μη διαθέσιμοι διακομιστές και τα προβλήματα με τους αυτοματοποιημένους ελέγχους υγείας…
items.descriptionOriginal: Microsoft is still working to restore services after a widespread outage disrupted access to Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft 365 applications. The disruption affected nearly 130,000 users globally, according to reports collected by Downdetector. Microsoft now believes unavailable servers and problems with automated health checks contributed to the incident. The software giant has started bringing affected infrastructure back online. However, some users continued experiencing connectivity problems as recovery efforts progressed Thursday. Server failures caused disruption Microsoft traced the disruption to an infrastructure problem that left several servers unexpectedly unavailable. Those failures increased the workload on remaining servers, creating additional pressure across its infrastructure. The company said overall traffic had not increased enough to explain the elevated load. Instead, unavailable servers forced the remaining infrastructure to handle more requests than usual. We're actively restarting and validating the affected servers to return them to service. In parallel, we're assessing whether reverting a small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery. More info under EX1550543 and MO1550821 in the… — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026 An issue with automated server health checks may have contributed to the problem. These checks help Microsoft determine whether individual servers are functioning correctly. However, a failure in that process apparently prevented some servers from remaining available. The resulting connectivity problems affected several Microsoft 365 products. Users reported difficulties accessing Outlook mailboxes and sending or receiving emails. Others struggled to load Teams and Microsoft’s productivity applications. Downdetector recorded nearly 130,000 reports during the outage’s peak. Reports covered Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and OneDrive. Microsoft’s Copilot assistant also experienced disruptions. Microsoft tests recovery measures Microsoft has begun validating an alternative health-check method to bring affected servers back online. The approach has already worked on a subset of impacted machines. The company is now expanding that fix across its affected infrastructure. It is also developing an automated process to identify unresponsive servers and restart them. Microsoft previously said it was restarting affected machines to restore availability. The company also paused deployments and configuration changes while investigating potential causes. Its investigation identified recent configuration updates as a possible contributor. Microsoft is now assessing whether reversing some of those changes could speed up recovery. In its latest update, Microsoft said it was actively restarting and validating affected servers. It also confirmed that engineers were evaluating whether reverting selected configuration updates would accelerate the process. The company has not confirmed that configuration changes directly caused the outage. Its investigation remains ongoing. Recovery remains underway Microsoft previously reported progress in restoring Teams services across North America. However, reports from affected users indicated that connectivity problems had not disappeared entirely. The disruption also exposed how failures within individual infrastructure components can affect several interconnected services. Microsoft’s cloud-based applications depend on extensive server infrastructure to handle authentication, communications, and data access. Automated health checks play an important role in maintaining that infrastructure. They help operators identify malfunctioning machines before those failures affect wider services. A problem with the checks themselves can complicate that process. Microsoft’s recovery efforts now involve restoring unavailable servers and examining recent infrastructure changes. The company has yet to provide a definitive explanation for the underlying failure. Users experiencing continued problems may still encounter intermittent access issues as Microsoft works through its recovery process.

items.descriptionOriginal: We like to think we always know the right thing to do. Some lessons, however, come the hard way . We learn through mistakes and missteps, stumbling into victories through trial and error. Some lessons, it seems, we have to learn on our own, no matter what other people have tried to tell us. There are also hard truths that come from quiet reflection or mulling over guidance passed down from a mentor . Now add random internet comment sections to that list. A popular Reddit thread recently asked users to share the one piece of advice that permanently altered their perspective. The responses offer a powerful reminder to listen closely to others’ wisdom. Here are 10 life-changing pieces of advice that might just reshape your own journey. 1. Ask which choice lets you be who you really are. “When I consider options, I ask which choice lets me become more of myself? It doesn’t mean ‘always choose whatever feels good.’ Sometimes becoming more yourself requires doing something difficult, disciplined, or terrifying.” We often make decisions based on comfort or fear. This may seem like the easier route, but is it more beneficial for you in the long run? Asking which path brings you closer to your true self shifts the focus completely. Growth rarely happens inside our comfort zones. 2. Never pass up an opportunity to use the restroom. ” It has NEVER failed me to be proactive.” Anyone who has ever been stuck in gridlock traffic knows the profound truth of this rule. Urgency doesn’t always lead to the best options. Proactive comfort is an underrated life hack. 3. Be forgiving; it sure helps. A quote often misattributed to various speakers (Buddha, Saint Augustine, Nelson Mandela, etc.) goes: “Holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die.” Whoever said it, the message is clear: forgiveness is as much for you as it is for the other person. No one is saying you have to forget, either. This is about freeing yourself from another person’s emotional baggage. 4. Accentuate the positive. “If you’ve spent years conditioning yourself to think negatively about yourself, you can condition yourself in the other direction too. It might feel cheesy at first but keep reinforcing the positive until that starts becoming your default mindset. Just embrace the cheesiness for now and do it anyway.” Neural pathways take time to rewire. Your brain believes what you tell it every day. Embracing a little cheesiness is a small price to pay to push yourself toward a more positive path. 5. Stop expecting everyone else to act like you. “Not everyone thinks like I do – and that’s ok.” This one hits deep. We often get hurt when people don’t react, work, or care the way we do. The spark of your passion does not have to be lit by others. Realizing that everyone operates from their own blueprint can save you lots of heartbreak. 6. It’s an expense, not a problem. “A problem that can be solved with money isn’t a problem; it’s an expense.” Perspective changes everything when life throws a curveball. A flat tire or a broken appliance can feel devastating in the moment, so don’t add fuel to the fire. Remembering that it is a financial hurdle, not a life-or-death situation, helps keep stress in check. 7. Nobody will thank you for living up to their expectations. “Stop people-pleasing.” No one wants to be someone else’s source of stress, but people-pleasing is a quiet trap. At the end of the day, you are the one who has to live with your choices. Live a life that makes sense to you. 8. How much time did you spend thinking about other people’s mistakes today? “It wasn’t much, right? I stopped caring so much about what others think of me at that moment. I started making more decisions without regrets.” We spend so much energy worrying about how others judge us. In reality, most people are too focused on themselves to worry about you most of the time. Recognizing this truth brings instant freedom. 9. Say no to some things so you can say yes to others. “Totally changed my POV. That was thirty years ago, and it has informed my successful career.” Understanding your limits is important, especially in business. Every single “yes” you give away is a hidden “no” to your own time and priorities. Protecting your energy ensures you have enough left for what truly matters, both at work and at home. 10. Empathy with boundaries is compassion. Empathy without boundaries is self-destruction. “Needed to hear this right now. Thank you.” There are plenty of things in this world that spark concern and worry. Compassion is what connects us , building bridges of understanding and community. But you cannot pour from an empty cup. Caring deeply for others should never require you to sacrifice your own mental health or safety. Give, but give what you can afford. The post People share 10 ‘random pieces of advice’ that legitimately changed their lives appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Psychologists say people who are always early aren’t rigid, they have 6 distinct personality traits
items.description: Τα άτομα που φτάνουν νωρίς σε συναντήσεις, ραντεβού ή hangout έχουν σαφώς καλές δεξιότητες διαχείρισης χρόνου . Αλλά μπορεί να υπάρχει ένας βαθύτερος λόγος για την αμεσότητά τους: καλλιεργεί μια αίσθηση ηρεμίας. «Το να φτάσετε νωρίς είναι ένας τρόπος να δώσετε στο νευρικό σας σύστημα λίγο χρόνο να προσαρμοστεί και να εγκατασταθεί», λέει στο Upw η Chloë Bean, LMFT, θεραπεύτρια σωματικού τραύματος στο Λος Άντζελες.…
items.descriptionOriginal: People who arrive early to meetings, appointments, or hangouts clearly have good time-management skills . But there may be a deeper reason for their promptness : it fosters a sense of calm. “Arriving early is a way to give your nervous system some time to adjust and settle in,” Chloë Bean , LMFT, a somatic trauma therapist in Los Angeles, tells Upworthy. “If you have anxiety around transitions or being in unfamiliar spaces, it gives you time to orient to your surroundings.” Being early may seem rigid to some, but for those who always arrive early, it’s not simply about needing control. “There is a distinct quality of an ‘early person’ having that need to have a level of control to actually remain flexible,” explains Nicole Issa , Psy.D., founder and licensed psychologist at The Center for Dynamic and Behavioral Therapy. “These sound polar opposite. But that ability to prioritize being early means they can probably cope very well when things don’t go to plan.” Their duality is one of the many unique personality traits they possess. Personality traits of people who are always early Besides seeking a sense of calm, these are six personality traits and strengths that people who arrive early also have, according to psychologists and therapists: Personality trait No. 1: They strive for emotional self-regulation Rather than just simple time management, Issa tells Upworthy that people who arrive early may plan like this to avoid last-minute pressures that leave them feeling out of control or frustrated because they’re late. “You might refer to this type of person as conscientious,” she says. “They might already know how they’ll feel if they’re the last to arrive, and it could be the driver for anxiety or stress, so avoiding that at all costs could very well become a priority for them.” Personality trait No. 2: They are reliable Arriving early also correlates with being intentional, Bean tells Upworthy. “This person shows up when they say they’re going to. You can plan your evening around plans with them because they take the commitment very seriously,” she says. “This makes them the friend or co-worker you can rely on every single time.” Personality trait No. 3: They are methodical “People who arrive early may have a methodical approach to everyday life,” Savannah Matlock, LCSW, a licensed clinical social worker, tells Upworthy. “This means that they tend to think through the steps needed to accomplish something and plan accordingly. They also may consider potential obstacles (like what could cause them to be late) and take action to avoid them.” Personality trait No. 4: They’re adaptable People who prefer to arrive early are also good at anticipating possible outcomes and mentally preparing for them. “They might not appear flexible at first, but if things suddenly change, they usually have a plan in mind that will cover it, meaning emotionally they remain calm and able to move quickly and still achieve their goal of arriving early,” notes Issa. “For some of us, the sheer prospect of a curveball can mean a meltdown.” Personality trait No. 5: They are empathetic People who arrive early are usually thinking about how arriving late will impact others—and how it will affect how others view them. “So, being late can mean trust is ultimately broken, or they might feel, ‘I just can’t rely on this person anymore,'” explains Issa. “Coming from this perspective does require someone to have consideration for situations and others. It could be as simple as someone planning to arrive consistently early to make sure they don’t hurt someone’s feelings. Or, in the case of meetings, they avoid any kind of backlash.” Personality trait No. 6: They like to have options Bean adds that being early also gives people a sense of choice. “They might spot the best table by the window or see a dessert shop they want to check out after dinner,” she adds. The post Psychologists say people who are always early aren’t rigid, they have 6 distinct personality traits appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: On their podcast Beyond the Nest , hosts Allison and Lance Welch share stories and insights from their grandparenting journey—everything from managing an empty nest to deepening intimacy once parental obligations have dwindled. In an episode titled “The Roles of Healthy Grandparents & Their Effect on Kids,” the two talked about a familiar family phenomenon: grandparents who seem to have a much more lax approach to rules than parents do…or than they did when they were raising kids themselves. In other words, “spoiling.” Interestingly, Allison shared a social media story that put a slightly sweeter spin on this common complaint. A second chance for softness In the post, a mother recalled confronting her own mom after she let her grandchildren watch cartoons on her phone, even though the kids weren’t allowed to do that at home. The woman asked, “ Why can’t you say no to your grandkids when you said it to me a million times growing up? ” Her mother had an answer that made her see the situation a little differently. She explained that becoming a grandmother gave her a chance to experience motherhood again, but with a little more perspective. “I’m experiencing the little version of you all over again, but this time with more patience and a gentle kind of love.” “ And then it hit me, ” the woman wrote. “The extra snacks, the screen time, the bending of rules, not breaking…it isn’t her going against me, but it’s her loving my kids so much that sometimes those boundaries blur. And maybe that’s the beauty of being a grandmother. That she gets to love without limits the way she wished she could the first time with me.” “This time, I get to love the little version of you with more patience and a gentler kind of love.” A grandmother’s response when her daughter asked why she lets the grandkids break all the rules she was never allowed as a kid. The extra snacks, screen time, and bending… pic.twitter.com/PDfCCcyXOT — Camus (@newstart_2024) May 30, 2026 That idea seemed to resonate with a lot of people A short clip of the podcast was shared on X, and grandparents and adult children in the comments shared similar thoughts on why the grandparent-grandchild relationship can feel so different from the parent-child relationship. One person wrote, “My father gave my daughter the time he hadn’t had for me. It was his redemption, and we both knew it. It healed our relationship better than any words.” Another commenter summed up the difference this way: “More simply, a parent must prepare the child for life. That requires sternness. A grandparent’s job is to show love and joy. The parents have the hard job.” Meanwhile, on TikTok , one grandparent shared, “Being a grandpa changed how I felt about rules…the job is to give memories before you’re gone.” Of course, there is a difference between a grandparent giving a child an extra treat and one who routinely ignores the parents’ boundaries. The former can be part of the joy of being a grandparent. The latter can create real tension for everyone involved. That distinction came through in the comments, too “I’m definitely a gentler grandparent than I was a parent. That said, I follow the rules set down by the parents. I spoil with extra undivided attention I couldn’t give as a working parent,” noted one viewer. View this post on Instagram In other words, when it comes to family dynamics, including grandparent relationships, there can be room for boundaries and for grace. This conversation certainly doesn’t settle the question of how grandparents should behave, and it probably doesn’t need to. Families will have their own rules, relationships, and boundaries. But the discussion does offer an interesting look at why the bond between grandparents and grandchildren can feel so different from the one between parents and children. It can also invite a bit more compassion during times of frustration. Watch the full Beyond the Nest episode below: The post A mom questioned why grandma ‘spoils’ her kids. The answer changed her perspective. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Sweet potatoes are a shining star of Thanksgiving . From sweet potato casserole to sweet potato pie , it’s versatile enough to serve as both a side and a dessert. Japanese food blogger Yuri Yamamoto has shared a recipe that calls for using Japanese sweet potatoes (called “ satsuma-imo “), ideal for a Thanksgiving feast. On X, she shared her easy recipe for “sweet simmered sweet potatoes,” which she called “a gentle treat.” With just five simple ingredients, they take less than 10 minutes to make. “It’s a classic recipe, but it’s super easy to make in the microwave, and it’s handy for snacks, desserts, and packed lunches,” she explained, before adding, “They have a flavor that’s unique to this time of year, so give them a try if you’d like .” 優しいおやつ、さつまいもの甘煮。定番レシピですが、レンジでめっちゃ簡単に作れておやつにもデザートにもお弁当にも重宝します。 フライパンにバターを溶かしてこんがり表面を焼いて食べたり、市販の絞るだけホイップとともにパンに挟むのも最高！！ この時期ならではの美味しさなので良かったら pic.twitter.com/spEO5IlyLZ — 山本ゆり（syunkon レンジは600W) (@syunkon0507) November 11, 2026 Japanese sweet potato simmer recipe Yamamoto offers several ways to prepare and enjoy her Japanese sweet potato dessert. “You can also melt butter in a frying pan, brown them on the outside, and eat them that way. Or sandwich them in bread with store-bought whipped cream that you just squeeze out—absolutely delicious!!” she wrote. Here’s how to make them: Ingredients 1 sweet potato 2 tablespoon sugar 1 tablespoon mirin 1/2 tablespoon soy sauce 150ml (about 2/3 cup) water Instructions Wash 1 sweet potato (200–250g) well. Cut it into 1-centimeter-thick rounds, and soak in water for about 5 minutes. In a microwave-safe container (a bowl works too), mix 2 tablespoons sugar, 1 tablespoon mirin, 1/2 tbsp soy sauce, and 150ml (about 2/3 cup) water. Loosely cover and microwave for 4 minutes. Flip over and microwave for 2 minutes (add 1–2 minutes if still firm). Let cool so the flavors soak in. If you like, you can add salted butter or margarine while it’s hot, or sprinkle on black sesame seeds—both are great! Refrigerate for 3–4 days. Adjust the sweetness to taste—more or less is fine. *You can also make this in a pot. (Use 200 ml of water, just enough to barely cover the sweet potatoes. Cover and simmer for about 6 minutes.) ①さつまいも1本(200〜250g)はよく洗い1cm厚さの輪切りにし5分程水にさらす ②耐熱容器(ボウルでも)に［砂糖大2、みりん大1(なければ砂糖を少し増やす)、醤油小1/2、水150ml］を混ぜ①を入れ、フワッとラップor蓋をずらしてのせ4分チン ③裏返して2分チン(固ければ追加1〜2分)。冷まして染み込ませる pic.twitter.com/sCktheLQkl — 山本ゆり（syunkon レンジは600W) (@syunkon0507) November 11, 2026 What are Japanese sweet potatoes? Although sweet potatoes are not native to Japan, they arrived in the island country from Central America sometime in the 1600s, according to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs . They experienced a cultivation boom in 1732 after the shogun (military commander-in-chief and leader of the country) encouraged the Japanese people to grow them to prevent future food shortages and famine. Japanese sweet potatoes typically have reddish-purple skin and yellow flesh. However, over 60 varieties of Japanese sweet potatoes exist today. In 2019, Bon Appétit food writer Sarah Jampel described one popular Japanese sweet potato variety, the Murasaki (which is seasonably available at Trader Joe’s ), as this: “They’re simultaneously drier and creamier than orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, which means that when you roast them at high heat (cubes, wedges, circles, or halves, simply coated with olive oil and salt and cooked between 425 and 450°), their edges get unbelievably crispy and burnished, belying the pudding-like centers.” However you prepare them, they will make a great addition to your holiday table. items.descriptionOriginal: Huddy Droubay had been waiting his turn. The 5-year-old from Syracuse, Utah, who has Down syndrome , watched his older brothers play soccer , and a little over a year ago, he finally joined a city league team himself. His mom, Melanie Droubay, posted a video of him out on the field. “The video got a couple million views because it was just him smiling the whole time,” she told KSL . “I don’t even know if he kicked the ball; he was just so happy to be on the field.” Serendipitously, one view came from superstar David Beckham. He commented that it was the sweetest smile he’d seen on a soccer pitch, or something close to it. “So, that was kind of the start of it all,” Droubay said. View this post on Instagram A few months later, Beckham sent Huddy a couple of signed jerseys with his name on them. Then, this past summer, a surprise package arrived with a letter from Beckham, now a co-owner of Inter Miami , inviting the whole family to a game. By then, Huddy had a name for him. His mother shared, “The ‘Mr. David’ part started when Huddy sang ‘Happy Birthday’ to David Beckham and sang ‘Happy birthday, Mr. David.’” On Wednesday, Oct. 28, before Inter Miami’s match against FC Cincinnati, the two finally met in the team’s locker room. In a video Droubay posted, Huddy hangs back for a moment before Beckham wins him over with a high-five and a hug. Beckham then takes his hand and gives him a tour, including a turn in Lionel Messi’s chair. They wore matching Inter Miami jerseys, and Beckham’s had “Mr. David” printed on the back. They signed each other’s shirts and went out on the field to score a few goals. View this post on Instagram The family thought that was the whole plan, but there was more. When the players came out of the tunnel before the game, Huddy walked out holding Messi’s hand. View this post on Instagram “We didn’t know that he was going to walk out with Messi,” Droubay said. “We just knew we were going to meet David Beckham and watch a game. (Beckham) went out of his way and orchestrated everything because I think he genuinely just wanted Huddy to have the best experience.” View this post on Instagram Droubay started sharing Huddy’s life online when he was born, on an account just for friends and family. Moments like this one, she said, mean everything. “I want Huddy to grow up knowing that he belongs everywhere, that he’s capable of amazing things, and that having Down syndrome doesn’t limit the joy and opportunities he deserves in life,” she said. View this post on Instagram The post How a young boy’s viral soccer videos led to an unforgettable day with David Beckham and Lionel Messi appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? Reading Time: 5 minutes How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? When you envision a typical construction site, you likely picture roaring diesel engines, towering waste bins and clouds of dust. However, forward-thinking builders are proving that heavy-duty work doesn’t have to create heavy pollution. While traditional operations take a massive toll on the planet through emissions and discarded scrap, you can drive real change on the ground. By embracing thoughtful equipment care, cleaner energy and circular material sourcing, your crews can build a greener world from the ground up. 1. Prioritizing Low-Emissions and Salvaged Materials Every major construction project begins with a blueprint, but the materials you specify in those early drawings dictate your build’s lifetime environmental footprint. Traditional supplies like standard Portland cement and virgin structural steel carry staggering amounts of embodied carbon—the hidden greenhouse gas emissions generated during raw material extraction, manufacturing, and transport. Many firms are swapping out carbon-intensive staples for lower-impact alternatives that still perform reliably. Mass timber, sustainably harvested from certified forests, sequesters atmospheric carbon right inside a building’s frame. Meanwhile, opting for supplementary materials, such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag — a recycled industrial by-product that can replace part of the cement in concrete — can significantly undercut the carbon emissions of traditional concrete mixes. Sustainability also means keeping things local and circular. By sourcing reclaimed lumber, crushed stone and recycled structural steel from regional deconstruction projects, you eliminate the fuel burned shipping heavy freight across the country. Salvaging high-quality elements prevents unnecessary virgin extraction, reduces procurement costs and gives historic materials a useful second life. 2. Adopting Proactive Machinery Maintenance to Reduce Waste and Boost Efficiency A truly sustainable jobsite isn’t just about what’s being built, but also about how efficiently machines run while building it. Proactive heavy equipment care is an essential pillar of low-impact construction. When diesel-powered machinery operates at peak mechanical efficiency, engines encounter less drag, burn significantly less fuel and prevent harmful oil leaks from threatening surrounding soil and local waterways. Routine inspections and precision adjustments prevent premature component breakdowns, keeping bulky metal and synthetic assemblies out of scrap heaps. Daily cleanings with a pressure washer clear away packed dirt and rocks that strain the undercarriage rollers, while maintaining proper track sag prevents engine strain and reduces excess fuel consumption. For example, checking the rubber tracks on skid steers to avoid wear and tear while encouraging optimal performance through proper tension reduces engine strain from overly tight tracks. Doing so means saving fuel and protecting components, leading to fewer emissions and a longer lifespan, which reduces manufacturing footprints. Prioritizing consistent preventive maintenance across excavators and loaders also curbs project delays and saves expenses. 3. Cutting Site Waste Through Circular Construction Practices Traditional construction projects generate mountains of debris, but progressive firms are more often viewing discarded materials as valuable future commodities. Moving toward a circular model begins with systematic on-site sorting, so instead of commingling off-cuts and packaging into generic roll-off dumpster bins, crews establish clearly labeled recovery stations for clean timber, scrap metal, cardboard and masonry. Processing materials directly where the work occurs can save significant hauling fuel and slash disposal tipping fees. Contractors often deploy portable rock crushers to break down clean demo concrete and masonry rubble on-site, producing quality sub-base aggregate to use for access roads, staging areas and sturdy foundation pads. When structures must come down, intentional deconstruction is replacing wrecking balls. Instead of demolishing older framing, crews carefully deconstruct timber and fixtures for repurposing in community projects or donation. Through active partnerships with local salvage yards and regional architectural reclaimers, firms keep large volumes of solid waste out of municipal landfills and help nearby communities access sturdy, character-rich, reusable materials. 4. Cleaning Up Fleet Power Heavy diesel machinery is a core part of commercial construction, but powering an entire fleet on fossil fuels carries a steep environmental and human price tag. Construction vehicles can emit substantial particulate matter and greenhouse gases, worsening local air quality while driving up fuel costs. Consequently, modern contractors are investigating ways to make fleet operations cleaner, quieter and more efficient. Electrification is leading this charge, especially among compact utility machinery. Battery-powered mini-excavators, electric wheel loaders and cordless hand tools deliver instant torque without generating smelly exhaust fumes or extreme noise levels. The shift to electric dramatically improves jobsite air quality, safeguards the respiratory health of on-site crews and earns goodwill from neighboring residential communities. Many larger diesel rigs cannot yet fully transition to electric powertrains, so operational discipline must bridge the sustainability gap. Establishing an automatic five-minute engine shut-off rule for loaders and haul trucks will reduce the exhaust fumes in the air while shaving gallons off daily diesel usage. Routine fuel tracking can ensure every engine runs at peak efficiency. 5. Leveraging Smart Planning and Modular Prefabrication Careful planning can make modern jobsites more efficient, with organized factory processes replacing crowded material storage areas. Modular prefabrication shifts significant building processes off-site into climate-controlled manufacturing facilities. In these organized plant environments, automated cutting systems reduce raw material scrap while optimizing usage down to the millimeter. Assembling wall panels off-site allows workers to recycle off-cuts and minimize on-site construction noise and dust. Simultaneously, modular construction eases neighborhood strain by slashing repetitive truck traffic. Instead of individual supply trucks trickling through local residential streets each day, preassembled building modules arrive in consolidated shipments. Digital project management platforms take this operational efficiency even further with advanced scheduling software accurately tracking incoming deliveries to ensure high-value lumber, drywall and delicate insulation arrive exactly when crews are ready to install them. As a result, there are fewer chaotic staging yards and likely a large reduction in expensive, weather-related material damage from heavy rain or exposure to damp ground. 6. Building a Jobsite Culture Around Everyday Sustainability Advanced equipment and green certifications certainly help, but authentic sustainability ultimately begins with people. Creating an eco-conscious jobsite means fostering a crew culture with daily habits that make resource conservation feel simple and worthwhile. The small decisions made throughout an ordinary shift quickly multiply across multi-month commercial developments. Simple operational swaps, like eliminating disposable water bottles in favor of refillable hydration stations and ditching single-use plastic wrap, drastically curb daily jobsite litter and establish an environmental mindset on the ground. Switching to energy-efficient LED lightbulbs in temporary site offices and encouraging shared crew transit foster an office and field culture in which eco-friendly choices become second nature. Sustainability-minded firms actively show their teams how these practical habits mirror broader everyday eco-friendly lifestyles. Incorporating simple sustainable living ideas into workers’ routines inspires tradespeople to make mindful, low-waste choices at home and at work. When crew members see company leadership genuinely backing these principles, green building becomes a shared source of pride instead of just a compliance task. Lay the Groundwork for a Cleaner Industry You can transform your construction operation into a more sustainable operation without overhauling everything overnight. True sustainability is an ongoing journey built on practical, everyday choices. By making each project cleaner, less wasteful and more efficient, you will make a tangible difference with every build. You hold the power to reshape the building landscape, proving that with each structure, you can construct a stronger, cleaner and more resilient tomorrow. items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the United States Department of Energy’s Ames National Laboratory discovered how to control the handedness, or chirality, of magnons. By changing a material’s magnetic states through the application of an external magnetic field, scientists gained the ability to manipulate magnon behavior, resulting in a substantial solution to a long-standing hurdle in physics. This discovery is paving the way for research into high-efficiency quantum computing and quantum information technologies. Magnons are elementary excitations of magnetic motion. As microscopic spin waves traveling through atomic lattices, magnons exhibit right- or left-handed motion, similar to how a spinning toy can rotate clockwise or counterclockwise. Since magnons transmit energy and digital information without the physical movement of electrical charge, they avoid the heat generation and power loss found in conventional electronics. Uncompensated sublattices in ferrimagnets ​The researchers investigated magnons’ handedness in ferrimagnets, a special type of magnetic compound in which both left- and right-handed magnons occur naturally. Ferromagnets possess spins with purely right-handed precession, whereas in antiferromagnets, materials characterized by the cancellation of opposing magnetic sublattices, left- and right-handed magnons are degenerate (sharing identical energy levels) unless an applied field splits them apart. Between the two are ferrimagnets, which contain two different types of magnetic atoms located in separate sublattices. Their respective magnetic moments point in opposite directions but have different magnitudes and therefore do not cancel each other out completely. The uncompensated spin moments of the sublattices give rise to both right- and left-handed magnon bands, separated in energy by internal molecular fields that exist within the compound. Crossing bands in Kagome metals ​A particular group of quantum materials that exhibit unusual magnetic behavior is known as Kagome metals. Their magnetic excitations were investigated at Ames National Laboratory by a team led by scientist Rob McQueeney, which focused its study on compounds such as TbMn₆Sn₆ and ErMn₆Sn₆. Researchers observed that in TbMn₆Sn₆, separate bands of left- and right-handed magnons cross at finite momentum without interacting. Conversely, in ErMn₆Sn₆, right- and left-handed magnons interact, opening an energy gap and preventing the crossing. ​Normally, left- and right-handed magnons require separate energy inputs and activation mechanisms for excitation. Researchers have also determined the exact momentum points at which the two states mix, based on the findings of Rob McQueeney’s group. ​Momentum-dependent chirality and quantum applications ​Depending on the symmetry of the ferrimagnetic order, band crossings either remain as nodal lines or become gapped. The scientists discovered how to manipulate this symmetry by changing the rare-earth magnetic anisotropy or applying an external magnetic field . Because the gapped modes contain hybridized chiral excitations, their net handedness depends directly on the magnon’s momentum. Hybridization makes it possible to switch a magnon’s handedness using a relatively small amount of energy. Controlling magnon handedness addresses a long-standing challenge in quantum materials research, the Ames National Laboratory researchers discovered. “Magnons have certain advantages for moving information,” McQueeney said. “But manipulating the handedness was not a solved problem. And now it is.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland have used a wood-burning stove to recreate wildfire smoke and uncover why nitrogen oxides linger far from the flames. Their lab experiments show brown carbon in the smoke speeds up the conversion of nitrate into nitrogen oxide tenfold compared with the known hard-UV process. The findings could improve predictions of how wildfires affect air quality and climate. The team was led by Markus Ammann of PSI’s Center for Energy and Environmental Sciences, with Fengxia Bao as first author. Smoke that travels far Wildfire plumes rise a few miles into the air and can travel across continents and oceans. Pollutants from wildfires in Canada can still be detected, for example, at the Jungfraujoch in the Swiss Alps. Those pollutants include particulate matter, carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which contribute to respiratory illness and, through the greenhouse effect, climate change. Ammann’s team wanted to explain why elevated nitrogen oxide concentrations persist even far from wildfires. An atmospheric puzzle Nitrogen oxides form during combustion. Wildfires and lightning are natural sources, but fossil fuel burning has pushed urban levels many times above pre-industrial ones. In the lower atmosphere, they help form ozone, a greenhouse gas and irritant, and oxidize to nitric acid, which dissolves as nitrate in aerosol particles. Rain then carries the nitrate to soil. That steady conversion should leave far less nitrogen oxide in the air than is observed. A reverse path exists: sunlight can turn nitrate back into nitrogen oxide through photolysis, but Ammann said it is “far too slow” to explain the amounts measured. One hypothesis was that something released during wildfires drives a second, faster photolysis route. Smoke from a stove Wildfires differ from other nitrogen oxide sources because incomplete combustion of wood and other biomass also produces organic particulate matter, including some soot. Some of those organic compounds absorb visible light and are collectively called brown carbon. To test its role, the researchers cut the air supply to a wood-burning stove to make more smoke and more brown carbon. They collected it on filters, dissolved it in water, and placed it in a temperature-stabilized glass tube. They then exposed nitrate to various UV lamps simulating sunlight, once without brown carbon and once with it, and measured the nitrogen oxide produced. Light with a high-energy, hard UV component always produced nitrogen oxide, but samples with brown carbon produced significantly more. With lamps lacking hard UV, nitrogen oxide appeared only when brown carbon was present, said Bao. The researchers concluded the route is indirect: brown carbon absorbs soft UV light, enters an excited state and donates an electron to nitrate, converting it to nitrogen oxide. That pathway accelerates nitrogen oxide production tenfold compared with the known process under hard UV light. What remains unexplained This is a “clear, powerful result,” Ammann said, one that shows experimentally what had only been vaguely suspected. The result explains a larger share of atmospheric nitrogen oxides, but not all, so other formation pathways need further research. Ammann wants to make the experiments more realistic, for example by using all of the burned material in PSI’s simulation chamber instead of only filtered, dissolved components. The work was funded by the ETH Board’s ReCLEAN project. The findings were published Nov. 11 in Science Advances .

items.descriptionOriginal: If you meet someone new and realize they have a dark sense of humor , you may see it as a red flag. It could suggest that they are moody, aggressive, or lacking in compassion. After all, doesn’t it seem mean-spirited to laugh at something traumatic, unsettling, or a joke that punches down? However, a study by the Medical University of Vienna, published in the journal Cognitive Processing , found the exact opposite. Cognitive and emotional demands of black humor processing: the role of intelligence, aggressiveness and mood says that people with a sick sense of humor are smarter, less aggressive, and less likely to be in a poor mood. Child making a practical joke. Crediy: Canva “These findings support the notion that humour processing depends on cognitive as well as emotional aspects, and suggest that this also accounts for black humour processing, which seems to be a complex information-processing task,” the study’s authors wrote . Why is a sick sense of humor good? It seems that a sick sense of humor is more about understanding humor and its ramifications than about appreciating the dark subject matter itself. It also shows you have the emotional maturity to feel comfortable with taboo and uncomfortable facts of life. It takes some self-development to laugh at things that many have a hard time even thinking about. Woman making a weird joke. Credit: Canva “So why the link between intelligence and enjoyment of black humour? One possibility is that you have to be clever to understand the joke, although most of the jokes were uncomplicated,” Ben Ambridge, Professor of Psycholinguistics at the University of Manchester, writes for The Guardian . “Perhaps more intelligent people are better able to rationalise away outrage—‘the existence of this joke does not harm anyone’—that might otherwise get in the way of their enjoyment.” The researchers showed 156 participants 12 cartoons by Uli Stein from The Black Book . Here’s an example of his work. “Do you have a reservation?” the receptionist asks his fellow worms as they try to chow down on a recently deceased corpse. New #cartoon book by Uli Stein: The Black Book: “Do you have a reservation?” pic.twitter.com/oXjyCqppQJ — Jürgen "jkr" Kraus (@jkr_on_the_web) August 3, 2022 What were the results of the study? After rating the participants on aggression, IQ, and mood, they found that those who enjoyed dark humor and understood it the best also ranked highest on verbal and non-verbal IQ. They also ranked low for aggressiveness and moodiness. Conversely, those with average verbal and non-verbal intelligence and high aggression and moodiness showed the lowest appreciation and understanding of dark humor. To put it simply: If you like sick humor, you’re probably smarter, better educated, less aggressive, and more even-tempered than those who don’t. Ultimately, if you meet someone new and they crack a sick joke and it immediately seems like a red flag, relax and enjoy it, because it actually means they have a lot of great qualities. “One thing is clear: given the negative link between black humour and aggression, anyone who argues that a mean sense of humour leads to meanness in real life must be joking,” AMbridge writes. The post A dark sense of humor doesn’t mean you’re gloomy. It actually reveals 3 surprising strengths. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: You might think people would prefer an interesting new story to one they already know. However, Harvard researchers found that listeners sometimes enjoyed familiar stories more than unfamiliar ones, even when the storytellers expected the opposite. The 2017 study, published in Psychological Science , found that knowing something about a subject can make a story more enjoyable. When people are already familiar with what happened, they can follow along more easily. Without that background, even a fascinating experience can be difficult to appreciate. Three women talk in a family room. Photo Credit: Canva Why did people enjoy familiar stories? Researchers conducted four experiments to explore how people respond to stories about both familiar and unfamiliar events. In one experiment, participants described a video they’d watched to someone else. Some listeners had already seen the video, while others had not. The storytellers expected people who hadn’t seen the video to enjoy hearing about it more. After all, the experience would be completely new to them. But the results showed the opposite: listeners who were already familiar with the video enjoyed the retelling more. The researchers called this phenomenon the “novelty penalty.” An unfamiliar story could lose its appeal when people struggled to follow what was happening. Three people talk at a table. Photo credit: Canva Why do storytellers get this wrong? One challenge of telling a story is that the person sharing it already knows how everything fits together. They know the people involved, the circumstances, and the little details that make it funny, suspenseful, or memorable. Their audience doesn’t necessarily have that background. As Gus Cooney, a study co-author and Harvard PhD student at the time, explained in The Harvard Gazette , storytellers can underestimate how difficult it is for someone else to picture an unfamiliar experience. “If I am telling you a story about Turkey or Thailand you may start to imagine it, but as the story goes on I start introducing new characters and new places and things that I’ve done, I think our imaginations can often fail us if we’ve never been to those places ourselves,” Cooney said. “Imagination is great, but it also has its limits,” he added. Familiarity helps listeners fill in the gaps. Even when a storyteller leaves something out, someone who already knows the subject can often understand what they mean. A young man shares his story. Photo Credit: Canva What makes someone a better storyteller? A 2024 study published in Cognition explored another side of storytelling. Researchers asked participants to describe a video game they had played. Some were told to recall everything they could, while others were asked to convey it as if telling a friend at a party. Researchers found that listeners enjoyed stories more when the storyteller used language that conveyed greater confidence. Including more general information about the game was also linked to greater interest in buying it. Both studies point to ways people can become better storytellers. The Harvard study highlights the importance of giving listeners enough background to follow along, while the newer research suggests that delivery can also influence its appeal. For everyday conversations, that means paying attention to what listeners already know, providing enough context to bring them along, and telling the story naturally rather than trying to make every detail sound extraordinary. Sometimes, making an ordinary experience entertaining is the more impressive skill. The post People expected to enjoy unfamiliar stories more. An experiment found the opposite. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Robert Kaplinsky is one of the most sought-after and referenced math educators in the world. He’s a longtime teacher who specializes in empowering students and encouraging deeper-level thinking. So it’s no surprise that he loves to challenge his students with difficult puzzles , logic tests, and riddles . Teacher challenges students with ‘nonsensical’ shepherd riddle Years ago, Kaplinsky shared a post on his blog about how he presented his students with an impossible puzzle. The question seemed simple enough: “There are 125 sheep and 5 dogs in a flock. How old is the shepherd?” Professor Katherine K. Merseth created the riddle in 1993 based on research conducted in the 1980s. Most students calculate a numerical answer to the problem It’s clear to most adults that the shepherd problem does not include enough information. The number of sheep and dogs has nothing to do with the shepherd’s age. He could be 25, 57, 80, or 102. The numbers provided in the problem are mostly unrelated. But that’s the trick of the problem. Kaplinsky had read the research and hypothesized that about half of his students would calculate an answer using the numbers presented in the problem. It turned out to be even more. Closer to 75% of students answered with a concrete number. What’s fascinating is that the kids ran the gamut, covering nearly every possible computation with the numbers 125 and 5. Kaplinsky writes:”2 students calculated the answer to be 130 (125 + 5) … 2 students calculated the answer to be 120 (125 – 5) … 12 students calculated the answer to be 25 (125 ÷ 5)” A couple of students just guessed, choosing not to calculate anything at all. There was just one student who very nearly got it. Only one student (almost) figured out the problem One of Kaplinsky’s students initially answered that the shepherd was 120 years old, the total they arrived at after subtracting the number of the dogs from the sheep. But then, Kaplinsky writes, the student realized that it couldn’t be correct and made a second attempt. “The student who got 120, then said that you don’t have enough information to figure out the shepherd’s age.” However, even though the student was so close to getting it, they ultimately guessed 90 years old. Kaplinsky says the student was “uncomfortable” with not providing an answer to the question. Professor Merseth writes in her essay that about three out of four schoolchildren will provide a numerical answer to the impossible problem, which matches Kaplinsky’s result exactly. She, too, found the most common answer to be 25—because 120 and 130 were considered too old. So what’s going on here? Why does this nonsensical riddle trip up so many kids, and what can we learn from it? Merseth’s paper addresses misconceptions students in America have about mathematics and why American kids routinely perform below many of their international peers in the subject. “In a child’s world, mathematics is seen as a set of rules — a collection of procedures, actually — that must first be memorized and then correctly applied to produce the answer,” she writes. “How frequently teachers see this eagerness to begin writing and manipulating numbers before the situation is fully understood!” It’s not the students’ computation that’s the problem. It’s their understanding of what the question is asking, given the information it provides. But even beyond that, it’s a question of something Kaplinsky calls “intellectual autonomy.” “Many of the students knew I was crazy for asking them this question, yet they felt like they couldn’t question the questioner and were obligated to answer me,” he writes. “So, they repressed that feeling and gave me an answer anyway. That’s certainly not where we want students to be.” Studies have shown this doesn’t just affect children. In the famous Asch Conformity Experiments , participants would willingly go along with an obviously wrong answer to a test if others in the room did. Funny enough, about 75% of volunteers felt pressure to conform; similar results to the shepherd problem. It takes courage to break from the pack or confront an authority figure when you think they’re wrong. Kaplinsky’s use of the shepherd problem not only encouraged the kids to think more critically and understand problems holistically before trying to solve them, but also taught them a valuable lesson in trusting their instincts. The post A teacher gave 32 eighth graders an impossible math problem. One kid’s second guess says so much. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Retirement is a time to take it easy, but Swedish gamer Abbe “DieHardBirdie” Borg is doing things a little differently. Since retiring, he has created a completely new life in his golden years through competitive video gaming . At 75, Borg started playing the shooting game Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO). He joined a team called the Silver Snipers, made up of fellow players all over 65. At 78, he became the world champion after winning the DreamHack 2019 competition with the Silver Snipers. At the time, Borg shared, “At 78 years old, I may be a bit older than most, but it’s never too late to learn something new. We do not know what might happen, but you might end up winning a championship or become a world-famous esports gamer.” Now on a team called the Golden Snipers , he continues to game at 83 . Gaming after retirement Before he retired, Borg was a professional artist for 50 years. He also did some modeling. “Before gaming, I was a commercial model for years—the senior face in Scandinavian ads,” he wrote on LinkedIn . “Then a mouse replaced the camera, and I became a world champion instead.” “I was in some commercials in Sweden,” Borg told USA Today in 2021. “That’s how Lenovo found me. Their first question was if I was interested in playing games—esports games. And I said, ‘Alright. I’m curious. I’ll do it if they will.'” His gaming nickname, “DieHardBirdie,” developed from his skills as “a virtuoso of bird calls and bird sounds.” Continuing to hone his gaming skills after his world championship, he joined the streaming platform Twitch in 2020. “I stream my game on Twitch because I like to leave something behind after my life, for the next generation,” he told PC Gamer . “[I]f someone tells me you have to stop playing, that’s impossible for me.” Positive benefits of gaming and aging Borg explained that being a gamer at an older age has come with many positives. One especially bright spot has been inspiring other retirees to start gaming to connect with younger generations. “I hope more elderly people will be watching esports and try to play,” he told USA Today . “We need to wake up their spirits, and ask them to find some guts to try and play, to find some support from their family, their children and grandchildren.” Additionally, Borg added that playing video games has benefited his physical and cognitive health. “This game helps me. My fingers go very fast now. I used to have pain in my fingers, but that’s no more,” he told the publication. “My coordination between my hands and eyes is very good. My reflexes are faster than ever. I feel good. And I find after playing, I’m not tired. It’s not about winning and losing. But this game helps me.” Borg also credits staying healthy at 83 to his consistent routine: “People ask how I keep my hands fast and my head clear at 83. Sleep. Movement. Practice every day. And the same 5 vitamins every morning — a simple routine, never skipped,” he wrote on LinkedIn . “That routine became my DHB vitamins. Healthy aging is not luck. It is a routine you keep.” “I still play about 4 hours a day. Age did not slow me down—it made me patient, and patience wins games,” he added . The post He took up competitive gaming after retiring. Then he retired again—with a championship. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Ο ερευνητής της ευτυχίας Δρ. items.descriptionOriginal: Happiness researcher Dr. Arthur Brooks says that one of the most important things people can do as they enter the second half of their life is to focus on internal well-being rather than satisfying all of their wants. Even though this may feel like it runs counter to how many live the first half of their lives, he says it’s the best way to find joy in middle age and beyond. Brooks is a professor at Harvard Kennedy School and Harvard Business School, author of From Strength to Strength and Build the Life You Want (with Oprah Winfrey) and is a lifelong student of the science of happiness . He says the key to finding it in the second half of life is recognizing when enough is enough and reducing unnecessary desires. “What happy, successful people do in the second half of their lives is they go from adding to subtracting,” Brooks says. “Mother Nature tells you that satisfaction comes from having more. More of what? More money, more power, more pleasure, more honor, more everything. More. But that’s not the secret. The real formula for happiness is all the things that you have divided by the things that you want.” It starts with looking inward For Brooks, finding happiness later in life is an inside job: we analyze our desires and decide which ones we can cast aside. It’s a worthwhile practice, given that as we age, our ability to achieve many of our desires is compromised by the aging process. “There’s two ways for you to get greater satisfaction,” Brooks continues. “There’s the old, inefficient way of have more, have more, have more. Or there’s the efficient, enduring way of wanting less.” It’s easy to tell people to manage their desires, but how do they come up with a strategy for doing so successfully? He says one way is to audit your desires by putting them to a simple litmus test. “One helpful exercise is to list your major goals and ask: Would this still matter to me if no one else knew I achieved it? If the answer is no, it may not be a goal rooted in meaning,” he writes on LinkedIn . Redefining what success even means Brooks also believes that we can simplify our lives by redefining what it means to be a success. “In research on midlife satisfaction, those who reoriented their ambition from status to service, especially men, reported higher purpose and deeper relationships over time,” he adds. Gratitude plays a role too Another meaningful way we can find greater happiness is by setting some of our wants aside and being grateful for what we have. Because if you aren’t grateful for the positives you have in life, they will never stick to your bones or be truly nourishing. “Practice gratitude for what you have,” Daniel Levitin , professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at McGill University, writes in Successful Aging . “This is motivating, alters brain chemistry toward more positive emotions, and oils the pleasure circuits of the brain.” There’s something graceful about accepting a new challenge in life as we get older: learning to have the internal strength to set aside what we truly don’t need and to nurture what we do, such as our relationships, friends, and community. Brooks’ perspective is a valuable tool that will keep many from being led astray as they age by chasing things they no longer need. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. items.description: Ο Chotu, 40 ετών, διευθύνει ένα pakori thela (πάγκο με τηγανητές) έξω από το ναό στο Lalbagh στο Moradabad. Έχει παρακολουθήσει τη σχέση των ανθρώπων με την κοντινή όχθη του ποταμού να αλλάζει. "Νωρίτερα, ο κόσμος παρακολουθούσε τους εθελοντές καθαρούς· σήμερα, οι ίδιοι οι ντόπιοι αισθάνονται υπεύθυνοι για τη διατήρηση του γκάτ και του ποταμού καθαρά", λέει. Για τον Kapil Kumar, 35, που ηγείται του Clean Up…
items.descriptionOriginal: Chotu, 40, runs a pakori thela (fritters stall) outside the temple at Lalbagh in Moradabad. He has watched people's relationship with the nearby riverbank change. "Earlier, people watched the volunteers clean ; today, local people themselves feel responsible for keeping the ghat and river clean," he says. For Kapil Kumar, 35, who leads the Clean Up Ram Ganga Campaign, this willingness to take responsibility matters deeply. His team at Parivartan "The Change" reports completing more than 218 clean-up drives and removing over 1.2 lakh kg of waste, with more than 5,000 volunteers participating over the years. Behind those figures are conversations with visitors, residents making space for equipment, and volunteers returning to a riverbank they have come to care about. Getting here took several attempts. A teacher's question took him beyond his textbooks Kapil completed his B.Tech in mechanical engineering in 2013 and spent a year in the automobile sector. From 2014 to 2016, he pursued a PGDM while preparing for government examinations, including the UPSC Civil Services Examination. His UPSC preparation continued until 2017. Kapil and his friends founded Parivartan in October 2016 and registered it in July 2017. "During my UPSC preparation, studying sociology helped me look beyond individual issues and understand society, communities and the factors that influence social change. It gave me a much broader perspective on the challenges people face," he tells The Better India . In 2016, blogs he wrote to practise essays and answers drew responses from juniors and former college colleagues. "They asked me, 'Why don't we do something on the ground?' And that's where it all began. We started with a few activities and gradually built from there," he recalls. A visit to a government school in Moradabad gave that suggestion a practical meaning. Kapil found leaking roofs, inadequate washrooms and children without proper chairs and benches. When he questioned the conditions, a teacher challenged him. "People usually come here for surveys and other work, criticise the government and the administration, and then leave. But what can you actually do beyond criticism?" he recalls her asking. She pointed him towards a child with an eye problem. "So she asked me, 'Can you take him to the hospital and help him get the treatment he needs?' I took that on," he recalls. Kapil contacted the chief medical officer and helped the child receive treatment and spectacles. "If you do something with genuine intention, without expecting anything in return, it gives you a different kind of satisfaction," he says. Kapil and his friends founded Parivartan in October 2016 and registered it in July 2017. Their early work included riverbank awareness, air pollution and women's empowerment through street plays and role plays. "There was no fixed project or particular cause in mind," he says. "We felt that we wanted to do something about social issues. So, we would meet, discuss what we could do, make a plan, and then take it to the ground." "It was largely a process of trial and error," he says. Some members left as they completed engineering or MBA courses and chose other careers. Kapil continued with a smaller team, gradually recognising that he wanted to work in the social sector. Why did the waste keep coming back? In November 2016, Kapil sat beside the Ramganga during a riverside festival, watching plastic bags, flowers, clothes and household waste enter the water. He began talking to visitors about what they were discarding. "We have a living river in our city. It was once the lifeline of the communities living along its banks. But today, industrial waste, sewage and all kinds of solid waste are being dumped into it," he recalls. The conversations showed him that people needed practical alternatives. The team explained how flowers and other organic offerings could be composted in a designated pit, while plastic and other non-biodegradable waste could go to municipal collection. Visitors responded positively. The team explained how flowers and other organic offerings could be composted in a designated pit. On Earth Day, 22 April 2018, the team formally launched the Clean Up Ram Ganga Campaign. Three months of Sunday clean-ups at a ghat (riverside steps) were followed by a wall mural and an 11,000-signature campaign. They carried the signatures on a cycle yatra (journey) from Moradabad to Varanasi, passing through Rampur, Bareilly, Shahjahanpur, Sitapur, Lucknow, Raebareli and Prayagraj. Yet the work at the riverbank exposed a problem. "What we were doing earlier wasn't sustainable," he says. "We would clean the ghat for three months, but once we stopped, it would eventually return to the same condition." Between 2018 and 2020, the team stayed involved through monthly engagement, festival clean-ups and awareness activities, without a fixed weekly schedule. COVID-19 then interrupted public activities. Parivartan worked with the district administration and volunteers to provide essential supplies to marginalised communities. Kapil also remembers seeing distant hills from Moradabad's rooftops during the lockdown, when the air was clearer. The experience reinforced his interest in sustained environmental work. "It made us realise that environmental work cannot be a one-time effort. The real difference comes when you keep showing up and continue the work," he says. This time, there would be no end date On World Environment Day, 5 June 2021, the team began a new phase at Lalbagh Ghat. Household waste and discarded offerings littered the bank, with few awareness messages or conversations about pollution. Kapil wanted the clean-ups to become a regular commitment. "We told our teammates and volunteers that this was not something we would do for a few weeks or months. We were in it for the long run, for the Ram Ganga," he says. In summer, volunteers generally work from around 6.30 am to 9 am; in winter, they start closer to 7.30 am. "We keep track of the numbers, document our progress and assess the impact to understand how the campaign is making a difference," he says. He says Sunday engagement has continued since then, with awareness activities replacing physical clean-ups when flooding or excessive rain makes the riverbank unsafe. In summer, volunteers generally work from around 6.30 am to 9 am; in winter, they start closer to 7.30 am. Kapil or a teammate briefs them before they begin. "All the volunteers come together with their gloves and other equipment," he explains. "I brief them on what needs to be done and what kind of waste we need to collect . If I'm not there, my teammates take over and guide everyone through the work." The focus is on plastic and other non-biodegradable waste. Depending on weather, season and footfall, a Sunday clean-up can yield around 300 to 700 kg, he says. The team segregates waste wherever possible. Flowers and organic offerings go into the composting pit. Recovered idols are kept out of the river. Other inorganic waste is handed to the municipal corporation for treatment and disposal, with recyclable material sent for recovery where possible. Alongside collection, volunteers speak to visitors about the available disposal facilities and ways to reduce waste. Those conversations have become central to keeping the bank clean. Changing a familiar habit takes patience "Behavioural change is a very tough thing," Kapil says. During the Navratri mela (fair), he estimates that 15,000 to 20,000 people visit the nearby temple each day, increasing the pressure on the riverbank. Some visitors told volunteers they were following practices passed down through their families. The team explained how they could continue observing their customs while using the waste facilities. Kapil says most visitors now use the designated pit or other disposal facilities. Announcements from the temple also encourage people to keep waste and offerings away from the bank, reinforcing the volunteers' message. On Earth Day, 22 April 2018, the team formally launched the Clean Up Ram Ganga Campaign. Mansi Mehrotra, 25, has been associated with Parivartan since December 2017. She joined after seeing waste around the river and recalls how much patience one conversation required. "Raising awareness was only the first step. We realised that real change would come only when we took action ourselves," she says. During a clean-up, she met a man planning to immerse plaster of Paris idols. He initially resisted her explanation of their environmental impact. The team continued talking to him, and eventually he took the idols back. "Sometimes, creating change requires patience, meaningful conversations and helping people understand why it matters," she says. Vikrant, 38, a waste collection vehicle driver with Nagar Nigam Moradabad, regularly visits the ghat and has witnessed the volunteers' work. "We have seen the change almost every week," he says. "The difference is clearly visible to the naked eye." "I have watched these youngsters working every Sunday for years, and their consistency has influenced me as well," he says. Giving people a reason to return The campaign's participants include students, professionals, residents, National Cadet Corps (NCC) and National Service Scheme (NSS) volunteers, and people from social organisations and community groups. Parivartan has more than 3,000 registered volunteers, while six full-time staff members work specifically on the Ramganga campaign. Kapil says staff join Sunday clean-ups as volunteers too. "Every Sunday we reach there because we consider it our social responsibility," he explains. The team also wants people to enjoy their time by the river. After a week in offices or colleges, volunteers can spend time outdoors, talk to vendors, and watch people farming and gardening nearby. There are pets playing, picnics, river festivals and stand-up sessions after clean-ups. "When people get the chance to come to the riverbank, take part in activities and observe the community around them, they really enjoy the experience," he says. Clean-ups also mark occasions such as Independence Day , Republic Day and Gandhi Jayanti. Over the years, participants have planted hundreds of trees, beautified public spaces and created awareness murals. The campaign received India Book of Records recognition for the "Longest Cleanliness Drive on a Riverbank Organised by an NGO". Kapil also sees its influence in volunteers' choices elsewhere. "I don't think any of these volunteers would litter on a riverbank, whether it is the Ram Ganga or any other river. Some of our volunteers are also involved in beach clean-ups in Mumbai, while others are part of clean-up efforts in Dehradun," he says. Old newspapers help pay for the next clean-up Keeping the work going requires funds as well as time. Through its SEHYOG initiative, Parivartan collects old newspapers, books, plastics and other recyclable material from households and well-wishers in door-to-door drives. The material is sold to authorised scrap dealers, and the proceeds help fund the organisation's social and environmental initiatives, including the Ramganga campaign. Individual donors and well-wishers contribute towards cleaning materials, awareness activities and other expenses. Local support also helps volunteers organise clean-ups when the core team cannot attend. "Even if no one from our team is able to come, you can still collect the tools and carry out the clean-up yourselves," Kapil tells them. Between 2018 and 2020, the team stayed involved through monthly engagement, festival clean-ups and awareness activities. Taking the river's problems to the authorities Kapil knows that removing solid waste addresses only part of the river's pollution. Untreated sewage needs action beyond the Sunday clean-ups. The team has submitted a 10-point action agenda and its 200-week campaign booklet to the National Mission for Clean Ganga and the State Mission for Clean Ganga. Kapil wants sewage treatment plants to function efficiently so wastewater from city drains is treated before entering the river. "The Ram Ganga is the tributary of the Ganga, and cleaning the Ganga is not possible without cleaning the Ram Ganga," he says. His ambition is a model ghat where people can visit, observe their customs and spend time by the water while keeping the surroundings clean. He says Sunday engagement has continued since then, with awareness activities replacing physical clean-ups when flooding or excessive rain makes the riverbank unsafe. "For us, the greatest achievement has never been the kilograms of waste removed from the Ramganga," he says. "It has been the change in people's behaviour." That change already has a place in Chotu's home, where the cleaning tools remain ready for whoever comes to collect them next Sunday. All pictures courtesy Parivartan "The Change".
