items.descriptionOriginal: Commonplace moments with a stranger can make all the difference in helping someone feel like they belong. You’re walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You’re tired, you’re leaving without the produce you came for, and you’re embarrassed. You pass by an older woman on the way out, steeling yourself for judgment. Instead, you get a knowing smile and hear, “We’ve all been there. You’re doing great, Mama.” And suddenly, you feel seen. Until recently, these sparks of connection didn’t have a name. Now, thanks to a University of Georgia researcher, they do: evanescent interactions. “What is communicated by these evanescent interactions is essentially, ‘You’ve noticed me. You’ve confirmed my existence. You’ve communicated that I am welcome here, that I belong here, that I have a place here, that I have value,'” says Joseph Hermanowicz, author of the publication and a professor of sociology at the University of Georgia. Hermanowicz defines evanescent interactions as brief moments when “strangers exchange gestures that create a ‘spark’ between them.” An evanescent interaction is more than just an ordinary exchange of pleasantries. These moments consist of brief but meaningful exchanges of mutual understanding and connection. “It’s important to be pleasant and kind to people, particularly in our present times, of course,” Hermanowicz says. “But I think it’s also important to recognize that when we do have a certain deliberateness with communicating with people, we could be accomplishing something very meaningful. We could communicate to people that they are important, that they matter, that we together form a community.” In his earlier research on the causes of undergraduate attrition, Hermanowicz found that evanescent interactions often influenced whether a student stuck it out or dropped out. Former students who dropped out says that a meaningful encounter with someone at the university who showed genuine interest in their well-being might have helped them feel more like they belonged. “In the absence of such contact, they felt alienated and not noticed, which fueled or did not impede a desire to leave,” he says. “So they left. “A lot of people are lonely. These sparks of connection can thwart feelings of not belonging in the various groups and organizations that we are a part of, whether those are friendship groups, work organizations, or society more broadly.” Evanescent interactions are brief, positive, and highly emotionally charged. They’re so ordinary that people may not give them a second thought. But they hold larger significance, Hermanowicz says. “Evanescent interactions are crucial to social life,” he says. “Two people communicating empathy to each other and recognizing each other as important holds extraordinary consequence. It affirms our mutual place in human community.” The article appears in Theory and Society . Source: University of Georgia The post How connecting with strangers can boost the sense of belonging appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Going to therapy does NOT mean you're mad. Yet, in many Indian families, seeking mental health support is still misunderstood, judged or dismissed. Actor Shefali Shah is challenging this mindset through her memoir, The Audacity of Being, where she opens up about mental health, depression and the importance of professional help. Her message is a reminder that sadness should never be dismissed and asking for help should never be a source of shame. It's time we stopped treating therapy as a taboo and started treating emotional health with the same importance as physical health. Seeking help is not a weakness. items.descriptionOriginal: There was a time when Gouthami Ravi and Sharan Kulkarni would have given anything to hear their daughter cry. Today, in their Bengaluru home, one-year-old Chikoo fills their days with little sounds, playful movements and the curiosity of a child discovering the world around her. She plays on the bed, makes her presence felt and gives her parents the kind of ordinary moments they once could only hope for. For months, they had watched over her breathing, learnt to manage medical equipment, and prepared for emergencies. A tracheostomy tube in her throat meant they could no longer hear her cry. Their home had become a medical care unit, and every day revolved around keeping their little girl safe. On 10 March 2026, after months of treatment, Chikoo's tracheostomy was finally removed. Sharan remembers that even before the procedure, he had held on to a belief that his daughter would survive. "We were not in a dilemma that it was 50-50 always. It was always 100%. She's going to survive," he says. That conviction carried the couple through a premature birth, frightening medical emergencies and months of round-the-clock care. But their experience also left them with a desire to help other families facing a similar journey. Born seven weeks premature, Chikoo weighed just 2.05 kg and needed breathing support soon after birth. When Chikoo needed a tracheostomy at barely a month old, they searched online for Indian parents who had been through the same experience. They found very little that could prepare them for what lay ahead. "I am so alone in this journey," Sharan remembers feeling. Today, Gouthami and Sharan want to make sure other parents facing a similar situation do not have to navigate it without guidance. They are open to speaking directly with families whose children may need a tracheostomy, sharing what they learnt through Chikoo's treatment and helping them understand what to expect. This includes practical guidance on questions to ask doctors, preparing a home for a child with a tracheostomy, learning tube changes and understanding how to respond to emergencies. They also want to be open about the medical, emotional and financial demands of long-term care, so families have a clearer picture of what lies ahead. While every child's medical needs are different and decisions must be made with the treating doctors, Gouthami and Sharan hope that sharing their experience can help another family feel less alone and better prepared. A premature birth, followed by an unexpected crisis Chikoo was born on 2 September 2025, seven weeks before her expected due date. Weighing just 2.05 kg, she needed breathing support and was moved to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) soon after birth. A stomach infection added to her early medical challenges. After around 15 days of treatment, she was discharged. Her parents brought her home, believing that the difficult beginning was behind them. "We thought it was the same way," Gouthami recalls, explaining how they assumed their daughter had recovered as many babies do after a NICU stay. They began settling into the routines of caring for a newborn: feeding, bathing, and looking after their little girl. Then, about a month into her life, something frightening happened. Chikoo's parents learnt to manage her tracheostomy care at home, from handling medical equipment to preparing for emergencies. During a feed, Chikoo began choking. Her skin turned blue, and she became unresponsive. Gouthami, who knew CPR, tried to help her while the family rushed to the hospital. Chikoo eventually began breathing again, and her oxygen levels appeared normal when they arrived. The family was sent home, with the episode attributed to a feeding issue. But when the same thing happened again about a week later, Gouthami and Sharan knew something was wrong. This time, Chikoo's oxygen levels began falling, and she needed sustained respiratory support. Further investigations revealed a combination of airway conditions, including laryngomalacia, a laryngeal cleft and tongue-base obstruction. Together, these were affecting her ability to coordinate feeding and breathing safely. The couple had entered a world of medical terminology, hospital admissions and decisions they had never imagined making for their newborn. The decision that changed everything As they began navigating unfamiliar diagnoses and difficult treatment decisions, the family relied on the guidance of their medical team. Gouthami and Sharan are grateful to Dr Sudheer K A, Dr Srikanta J T, Dr Antony George and Dr Priyanka Potti, Dr Vikas Satwik and Dr Sneha Lingappa, and Dr Shwetha Anand Baratikke from the pulmonary, paediatric, and gynaecology departments. The family credits the doctors involved in Chikoo's care for helping them navigate a period filled with uncertainty and decisions they had never expected to make. Gouthami and Sharan spent months learning the practical aspects of tracheostomy care so they could look after their daughter safely at home. As Chikoo continued to need breathing support, doctors recommended a tracheostomy, a procedure in which an opening is made in the neck to provide an airway through a tube. For a baby barely a month old, it was an overwhelming prospect. The first attempt was unsuccessful. The family had already been through the fear of watching their daughter struggle to breathe and the weight of agreeing to a major procedure. Now, they had to find the strength to try again. The second tracheostomy, performed in October 2025, was successful. But the procedure was only the beginning of another demanding phase. Chikoo needed time to recover and gradually come off the ventilator and oxygen support. Her parents spent weeks waiting outside the NICU, looking for updates and hoping that each day would bring progress. "Emotionally, we were too down," Gouthami says, describing what the family went through. With a suction machine, pulse oximeter and feeding pump at home, the family adapted their everyday routines to meet Chikoo's medical needs. They were also thinking about Chikoo's future. Gouthami wanted to understand whether her daughter would be able to develop and live as other children did. The family sought medical assessments, including checks on her neurological responses, and held on to the reassurance that these results offered. For Sharan, the answer was to keep believing in his daughter , even when the outcome was uncertain. "I never asked God for anything else," he says, describing how he imagined a future in which Chikoo would grow up and experience life beyond the hospital. That belief did not make the difficult days disappear. It gave them something to hold on to as they navigated one decision at a time. When home became a medical care unit After months of hospital care, Chikoo was eventually able to return home with her tracheostomy in place. But bringing her home did not mean returning to normal life. The family had to prepare their house for her medical needs, arranging equipment such as a suction machine, a pulse oximeter and a feeding pump. They also changed their daily routines to reduce potential irritants in the air. With nurses working in shifts, Gouthami and Sharan ensured Chikoo received the care and attention she needed at home. For months, they avoided lighting incense and made special arrangements for cooking. Nurses cared for Chikoo in shifts, with a dedicated space arranged for them at home. Yet Gouthami and Sharan knew that professional help could not always be immediately available. They therefore underwent practical training to learn how to care for the tracheostomy and respond to emergencies. "We had a booklet given. We had to read through that, do the Google research and go back the next day and explain what it is about," Gouthami recalls. The training lasted around 20 days. They learnt the procedures, familiarised themselves with the equipment and prepared themselves to manage situations that could arise at home. Learning to care for Chikoo at home also meant learning to trust their own hands while knowing when to seek medical help. The couple remains grateful to the medical team for guiding them through the practical aspects of her care and helping them prepare for emergencies. Their home nurses, Amina Ajusha and Aditya Sivadas, were also part of the support system that helped the family manage Chikoo's daily needs. Every 15 days, the family travelled back to the hospital for a tracheostomy tube change, carrying the equipment Chikoo depended on. They also had to learn how to perform the change themselves under medical supervision, knowing that they might need to act in an emergency. From monitoring her breathing to managing medical equipment, Chikoo's home-care routine required constant attention and coordination. Work had to find its place around these responsibilities. Gouthami was able to draw on maternity leave, while Sharan reorganised his business so that much of his work could be managed from home. His team supported him, allowing him to attend to his daughter while keeping the business running. The couple also leaned heavily on their families. "The need for having parents at home is extremely important," Sharan says. "Even today, without them, we cannot stay at home even one day." Gouthami credits her employer, SAP, for supporting her through this period. "SAP stood by me like family. The medical insurance and mental-health support gave me the confidence to make financial decisions for my daughter's care. I am endlessly thankful to my company for being there for me when I needed that support the most," she says. Chikoo's nurses became an important part of the support system that helped the family navigate life after her hospital discharge. The financial demands of Chikoo's treatment were considerable. From her hospital care and medical procedures to the home-care arrangements she needed until her tracheostomy was removed, the family spent approximately Rs 35 lakh. The family's personal health insurance covered only a part of the total expense, leaving them to manage the remaining costs alongside the demands of her care. The day they heard her voice again For months, Chikoo's parents had been unable to hear her cry with the tracheostomy in place. Before the tube could be removed, she underwent a series of carefully monitored steps, including a speech-valve trial and a capping trial to assess her ability to breathe through her nose and mouth. For Gouthami and Sharan, hearing Chikoo cry again was an emotional moment after months of being unable to hear her voice because of the tracheostomy tube. The process required patience. Chikoo did not immediately tolerate every step, and there were moments when the family had to wait longer than expected. Rather than rushing, they followed the medical team's guidance and gave her the time she needed. Then came a moment they had been waiting for. "When we were cleaning the tracheostomy, she started crying, and we could hear her voice," Sharan recalls. It was a sound that meant far more than words could express. The family and the nurses who had cared for Chikoo were moved to tears. After the trials and necessary medical assessments, her tracheostomy was permanently removed on 10 March 2026. Sharan remembers that no words could describe the moment. They went to the doctor and thanked the medical team. Looking back, he says, "It is not about being right here. It is about taking the next step." Today, Chikoo attends daycare, plays with toys and spends her days exploring new experiences as her parents watch her grow. Today, watching Chikoo play, vocalise, and grow, they can see how far she has come. She now goes to daycare, where she spends her days surrounded by bright toys, new little friends and plenty of activity. While a few developmental milestones are still catching up, her parents describe her as curious, energetic, and full of life. The medical equipment and routines that once dominated their lives no longer define every moment of their daughter's day. If you are a parent looking to connect with Gouthami and Sharan, you can reach out to The Better India team for their contact details or connect with them directly through their Instagram accounts. All images courtesy of Gouthami and Sharan.

items.descriptionOriginal: Every geological epoch leaves signatures. One of the Anthropocene’s may be a noise. Oceans echo with the drone of ship engines and blasts of sonar. Cities and suburbs roar with speeding cars and revving motorcycles. Even remote wilderness hums with passing airplanes and strolling hikers. Humanity has turned up the volume on the whole planet. That soundtrack is far reaching. New research in Science finds that noise pollution more than doubles death rates among wild animals. It is also rewriting the rules of who eats whom. In noisy places, prey grow jumpy and predators go hungry. Sometimes an animal fleeing the din runs straight into danger. Noise, the authors write, “reshapes the acoustic arms race” between species, and it creates winners and losers. The researchers argue that protecting wildlife in the Anthropocene means protecting quiet. “This work shows that noise pollution is an underrated threat to wildlife worldwide,” said Hansjoerg Kunc , an ecologist at Queen’s University Belfast and the paper’s lead author. Soundscapes, he said, should be safeguarded with the same seriousness as forests, wetlands and other physical habitats. Scientists have long known that noise harms living things. The World Health Organization calls it a serious health hazard for people: it shortens lives, impairs children’s brain development and disrupts sleep. What was missing was the big picture. Kunc and Queen’s colleague Rouven Schmidt gathered 214 studies examining noise effects on 177 species across six continents, from tiny beetles to hulking whales. They focused on controlled experiments, which can more reliably pin effects on noise itself. The effects were widespread. Noise was tied to fetal deformities, weakened immune systems and elevated stress hormones. It altered body size, feeding and parenting, and it changed animals’ success at hunting or escaping hunters. Pooled across the experiments, noise raised mortality by 138%. If 10 in every 100 animals would die in a world without human noise, 24 would die in a world with it. That’s large enough, the authors say, to “threaten population viability.” The effects on how species interact may matter just as much. Animals tended to steer clear of noisy areas, so their numbers there were 37% lower. The prey that remained were on high alert. So predators in noisy places caught 25% less prey, even though they worked harder to find it. But noise doesn’t necessarily help prey either. A loud sound might send a prey animal into a burrow or other enclosed space to hide. Those close quarters can amplify the noise, and that can flush the animal back into the open, where a predator is waiting. The fix, the researchers suggest, starts with treating sound as part of habitat. Kunc points to “measures such as low-noise zones that give animals a genuine acoustic refuge.” In an epoch defined by human influence, quiet may be one of the habitats most worth saving. items.descriptionOriginal: At 7 am in Delhi, the morning commute could become a visibility test over the next couple of weeks. In Lucknow and Patna, similar scenes play out as winter fog settles over roads, neighbourhoods and railway tracks, sometimes remaining until late morning. Now picture a winter morning in Bengaluru or Hyderabad . The temperature may have dropped overnight, and residents may step out wearing jackets, but the city is unlikely to wake up under the same blanket of persistent fog. So, if both regions experience winter, why does one see frequent spells of dense fog while the other experiences it far less often? The answer lies in more than temperature. Geography, moisture in the air, wind speed, overnight cooling and atmospheric conditions determine whether fog forms, how thick it becomes and how long it stays. Research by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and other climate scientists offers a closer look at why winter fog varies across India. Why the northern plains wake up under fog The Indo-Gangetic Plains, stretching across Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal, are among India's most fog-prone regions during winter. 🚨 Anti smog gun is now being used to spray water to mitigate air pollution. Visuals from Delhi, Ring Road near AIIMS. https://t.co/AWXJMn9NQC — Mumbai Rains (@rushikesh_agre_) November 9, 2026 An IMD research paper, Study of Winter Fog Over Indian Subcontinent: Climatological Perspectives , published in the journal MAUSAM in January 2014, examined winter visibility patterns across the country using meteorological observations. The researchers, G K Sawaisarje and colleagues, found that the Indo-Gangetic Plains experienced an average of seven to 10 foggy days in December and more than eight days in January. The region also had conditions particularly favourable for fog formation. Between December and February, average wind speeds were around 0.6 metres per second, temperatures ranged from 9 C to 15 C, and relative humidity stayed between 72% and 84% during the observations. But what makes these conditions important? Much of the fog across northern India is radiation fog. It forms when the ground loses heat overnight, cooling the air immediately above it. When this air reaches its dew point, the moisture present in it condenses into tiny water droplets, creating fog. Clear skies, sufficient moisture, and light winds allow this process to continue. When winds are too strong, the air mixes with warmer layers above, making it harder for fog to develop and remain close to the ground. Delhi, Lucknow and Patna: What the numbers reveal A 2023 study published in the International Journal of Climatology, titled Fog Trends in India: Relationships to Fog Type and Western Disturbances, examined three-hourly meteorological observations from 69 locations across India between 2000 and 2020. Researchers Daniel K E Smith and colleagues identified 10,262 fog events and found that radiation fog accounted for 68.1% of all events and 70% of dense fog events. The study also recorded an average of 54 fog events annually in Delhi, 45 in Patna and 39 in Lucknow. It identified statistically significant increasing trends in fog frequency in all three cities over the periods examined. Another factor influencing these conditions is the movement of western disturbances — weather systems originating around the Mediterranean region and travelling eastwards towards India. These systems can bring moisture and alter atmospheric conditions over northern India. In Delhi, 46.9% of radiation fog events beginning in December and January coincided with an active western disturbance. Kolkata's fog follows a different clock Move eastwards towards Kolkata, and the pattern begins to change. A September 2023 study published in Urban Climate, titled Event-Based Fog Climatology and Typology for Cities in Indo-Gangetic Plains , examined half-hourly visibility observations from seven cities between 1991 and 2020. The researchers, Prasad Deshpande and colleagues, found that fog onset followed an east-to-west pattern, with western cities experiencing delayed onset. Fog intensity, meanwhile, followed a north-to-south pattern, with northern cities recording more intense events. Kolkata, located near the mouth of the Ganga and influenced by its coastal setting, experienced relatively shorter fog events. Unlike the other cities studied, fog in Kolkata generally dissipated earlier, between 8 am and 11 am. The city also recorded a smaller proportion of very thick fog events. The Deccan's elevated terrain, varying moisture availability, and different patterns of atmospheric circulation create conditions that are generally less favourable for widespread, prolonged winter fog Photograph: (Indian Express) Across the seven cities, January recorded the highest proportion of fog events. Around 61% began between 8 pm and 5 am, while approximately 70% dissipated between 9 am and 1 pm. Why the Deccan experiences less persistent fog The Deccan Plateau is not entirely free from fog. The 2014 IMD study documented significant fog occurrences in South Interior Karnataka. Coastal Karnataka also recorded an average of approximately 6.5 foggy days during the winter season. The Deccan's elevated terrain, varying moisture availability , and different patterns of atmospheric circulation create conditions that are generally less favourable for widespread, prolonged winter fog than those across the northern plains. Fog Vs Smog However, fog and smog are not the same. Pollution can reduce visibility even without the atmospheric conditions required for meteorological fog. When pollutants mix with fog droplets, they can also contribute to persistent winter haze. Urban heat-island effects, changing aerosol concentrations, and atmospheric circulation can interact in complex ways, making it difficult to attribute changing fog frequency to a single cause. Ultimately, India's winter fog is not one uniform weather phenomenon. Delhi's frequent radiation fog, Kolkata's shorter morning spells and the relatively rare fog events across much of the Deccan reflect how local geography and atmospheric conditions shape each city's winter. Understanding these differences matters beyond predicting the morning commute. Fog affects road safety, railway and aviation operations, while the interaction between fog and pollutants has implications for air quality and public health. Sources: 'Fog Trends In India: Relationships To Fog Type And Western Disturbances' : By Daniel K. E. Smith, Stephen R. Dorling, Ian A. Renfrew, Andrew N. Verma, Published On 18 August 2023 'Study Of Winter Fog Over Indian Subcontinent : Climatological Perspectives' : G.K. Sawaisarje, P Khare, C.Y. Shirke, S. Deepakumar, N.M. items.descriptionOriginal: Every day, vegetable peels, leftover food and other kitchen scraps find their way into garbage bins across Indian homes. Once collected, much of this biodegradable waste ends up in landfills, adding to the country's growing waste management problem. But what if this waste could be turned into manure within 24 to 48 hours, right where it is collected? Kitchen scraps are sorted and prepared before being broken down into manure through a microbial process. That is what Nisargruna, a waste-processing technology developed by Dr Sharad P Kale, a scientist at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), aims to do. Already being used in Goa, the technology converts one tonne of kitchen waste into around 150 kg of nutrient-rich manure. Turning a tonne of kitchen waste into manure in two days The process begins with separating food waste, including vegetable peels and leftover food, from plastic and other dry waste. The biodegradable waste is then cut into tiny pieces before a special mixture containing microorganisms is added. These microorganisms break down the organic matter naturally, while air is supplied to speed up the process. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) Within 24 to 48 hours, the waste is converted into manure that can be used to n ourish plants and soil. Unlike conventional waste disposal systems that transport garbage to distant dumping grounds, Nisargruna allows the entire process to take place at the point where the waste is collected. This means kitchen waste can be treated locally instead of being mixed with other garbage and sent to landfills. Treating food waste close to home India generates around 78 million tonnes of food waste every year. When biodegradable waste is mixed with plastic and other discarded materials, managing and recovering useful resources becomes harder. Nisargruna offers a way to handle this problem at the source. Nisargruna enables communities to process their kitchen waste locally, reducing the amount of garbage that needs to be transported to landfills. By processing wet waste locally, the technology can reduce the amount of garbage that needs to be transported to landfills. It can also mean fewer garbage trucks on the road and cleaner dry waste, making it easier to recover and recycle materials such as plastic. The manure produced in the process can also find use in gardening and soil enrichment, giving discarded food scraps another purpose. Could more Goan villages turn their food waste into manure? The technology's journey in Goa began in Bicholim, where Nisargruna was first implemented. Now, plans are underway to set up these units across municipalities and village panchayats in the state, taking decentralised waste processing to more communities. First implemented in Goa, the technology is now being considered for wider adoption across the state's municipalities and village panchayats. Photograph: (X/@ The Logical India ) For cities and villages dealing with mounting piles of mixed garbage, the idea offers a practical alternative: instead of transporting every bit of waste elsewhere, process what can be reused where it is generated. A vegetable peel need not end its journey in a landfill. With the right process, it could return to the soil as manure within just two days.

items.descriptionOriginal: As Delhi wakes up to another morning of polluted air, a layer of dust settles on cars, windows, and balcony railings. However, amid the haze, money plants continue to trail down walls , marigolds bloom in pots, and hibiscus plants put out fresh leaves. Their survival raises a question for anyone who tends a balcony garden. How do plants continue to grow when the air around them is so polluted? Are some plants better equipped to withstand poor air quality, and what can gardeners do to help them cope? The question has become particularly relevant after Diwali. On the night of 8 November, Delhi's AQI reportedly climbed to 2,283, according to real-time readings cited by The Times of India . The official Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) average for Diwali day stood at 376. By 11 November, the city's AQI was around 301, in the 'very poor' category, according to Business Standard. Plants face the same polluted conditions, but their ability to survive depends on the species, duration of exposure, and growing conditions. How does polluted air affect plants? Plants need sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to grow. Their leaves absorb light and exchange gases through tiny openings called stomata. Dust and particulate matter settling on leaves can interfere with these processes, affecting the light reaching leaf surfaces and the functioning of stomata. As Delhi wakes up to another morning of polluted air, a layer of dust settles on cars, windows, and balcony railings. Photograph: (Invest India) Prolonged exposure can also affect photosynthesis and plant growth, as research on particulate matter and plant physiology explains. A high AQI reading does not mean every plant will immediately wilt. Some plants may continue to put out new leaves and flowers even as dust accumulates on their foliage, making regular care important. Which plants can tolerate polluted conditions? Researchers use the Air Pollution Tolerance Index (APTI) to assess how plants respond to pollution. It considers factors such as leaf pH, chlorophyll content, relative water content, and ascorbic acid levels. An Indian study of plant species in Delhi included Dracaena deremensis and Tagetes erecta, commonly known as marigold, among the plants examined. Both were classified as pollution-tolerant in the study. 1. Marigold Marigold is a practical option for a sunny balcony. It grows well in containers and produces bright flowers. Give it sufficient sunlight and well-draining soil, and avoid keeping its roots constantly wet. The Royal Horticultural Society's container-growing guide explains how to choose suitable conditions for potted plants. 2. Dracaena Dracaena is an option for an indoor or semi-shaded spot. Grown for its foliage, it can adapt to indoor conditions when it receives suitable light and is not overwatered. 3. Neem, peepal, and Pongamia For larger terraces or open spaces, neem, peepal, and Pongamia are worth considering. A research paper by The Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences examines pollution tolerance in tree species, including peepal and Pongamia. These trees are not practical for most small balconies, but may suit larger outdoor spaces. Pollution-tolerant does not mean pollution-proof. Severe or prolonged exposure can still affect plant health. Why balcony plants may struggle even without pollution Polluted air is only one possible reason a balcony garden may deteriorate. Seasonal changes and everyday care also matter. Winter temperatures and shorter days As winter sets in, shorter days bring less sunlight, while lower temperatures can slow plant growth. Cold drafts and sudden temperature changes may damage sensitive plants. With growth slowing, plants usually need less water. The Royal Horticultural Society's winter-care advice recommends moving plants to brighter spots, keeping them away from cold drafts and avoiding overwatering. Plants face the same polluted conditions, but their ability to survive depends on the species, duration of exposure, and growing conditions. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Too much or too little water Overwatering can leave roots sitting in water and lead to root rot. But letting soil dry out completely for long periods can also damage a plant. Check the soil before watering instead of following a fixed schedule. The University of Maryland Extension explains how excess water damages roots and causes leaves to yellow or wilt. Poor drainage and cramped pots Pots without drainage holes can trap excess water. Small containers can also restrict root growth, while compacted potting mix makes it harder for water and air to reach roots. Choose pots with drainage holes and repot plants when they outgrow their containers. Insufficient sunlight A flowering plant that needs direct sunlight may struggle to grow or produce flowers in a shaded corner. Without adequate light, plants may develop weak, elongated stems, pale or yellowing leaves, and fewer blooms. Before choosing a spot, check whether the plant needs full sun (at least six hours of direct sunlight), partial shade (around three to six hours of sunlight), or indirect light. Also, observe how sunlight moves across your balcony or garden during the day. A spot that receives morning sunlight may suit some plants better than one exposed to harsh afternoon sun. A little care can help plants cope During periods of heavy pollution, dust can build up on leaves, especially on balconies facing busy roads. Gently wipe broad leaves with a damp cloth or rinse suitable outdoor plants with clean water. Research on how leaves capture airborne particulate matter examines how particles collect on leaf surfaces. A flowering plant that needs direct sunlight may struggle to grow or produce flowers in a shaded corner. Photograph: (Greenway Biotech) Check plants for yellowing leaves , dry edges, and drooping stems. These symptoms do not always indicate pollution damage; they can also point to watering problems, inadequate light, or temperature stress. Balcony gardens cannot protect residents from Delhi's polluted air or make outdoor air safe to breathe. But choosing plants suited to the balcony and adjusting care as the seasons change can help them remain healthy, even when conditions outside are difficult.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News FireSat Satellites Begin Delivering Twice-Daily Wildfire Data Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes FireSat, a satellite constellation built for wildfire detection, launched its first operational satellites in July 2026 and began delivering twice-daily fire data worldwide. FireSat, a satellite constellation built specifically to spot wildfires, reached orbit for the first time as an operational system in July 2026. SpaceX launched three satellites from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California aboard a SpaceX rocket. Within two hours, all three had established contact with ground teams, marking the system’s shift from demonstration to active service. The constellation comes from Earth Fire Alliance , a nonprofit coalition built around a single goal: catching wildfires earlier than existing satellites can. Most space-based fire detection today relies on instruments designed for weather or general Earth observation. FireSat was engineered from the ground up for one job, drawing on interviews with more than 200 firefighters, incident commanders, and scientists worldwide. That focus shows up in the hardware. FireSat’s sensors can detect a fire as small as five meters by five meters, roughly the size of two parking spaces. Six imaging channels across five spectral bands work together to separate real fires from false alarms, keeping the error rate under five percent. A second midwave infrared channel addresses a specific technical problem. A single sensor can essentially overexpose when pointed at an extremely hot fire, much like a camera struggles with a bright light source. The extra channel is tuned to stay accurate even at the highest temperatures. These three satellites currently revisit the world’s most fire-prone regions at least twice daily. Earth Fire Alliance plans to shrink that gap to about one hour by 2029 as more satellites join the constellation. A full build-out of more than 50 satellites, targeted for 2030, would bring worldwide revisit times down to 20 minutes or less. Early results are already circulating. In September 2026, the team released its first active-fire images from the operational satellites, captured roughly three weeks after launch. Earlier tests with a single demonstration satellite had already caught a small roadside fire in Oregon that existing systems missed entirely. That demonstration satellite, launched in March 2025, spent more than a year in orbit proving the sensor technology before the operational constellation followed. During that period, it also captured thermal activity unrelated to wildfires, including a volcanic eruption and gas flares at an oil field, showing the instrument could distinguish between different types of heat sources. Those early tests gave engineers confidence to move from a single prototype to a working constellation. A wildfire burns through forested terrain at dusk, the kind of early-stage blaze FireSat is designed to catch before it spreads. Photo by Pixabay on Pexels. Beyond raw detection, FireSat tracks how a fire grows and moves once it starts. Data on a fire’s perimeter, spread direction, and radiative power feeds directly into incident commanders’ decisions. That kind of detail can shape evacuation orders and help responders decide where to send limited crews and equipment. Faster detection also offers a real cost benefit. Published research suggests that a one-hour revisit rate across the United States alone could help avoid more than a billion dollars in fire damage annually. Projections also point to roughly 3,500 homes protected and 21.9 million tons of carbon emissions prevented each year once the system reaches that pace. The project has been funded by a mix of philanthropic and corporate backers, including the Bezos Earth Fund, Google.org, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. Fire agencies such as CAL FIRE and research partners, including the Environmental Defense Fund, joined an early adopter program to help shape how the data is delivered. That early input helped earn the project a TIME Best Invention of 2025. Access to the data remains a central question as the system scales up. According to Earth Fire Alliance, the goal is to make FireSat data available to any fire agency, scientist, or community that needs it, not only wealthy nations with existing satellite programs. Whether that goal holds up as the constellation grows will shape how evenly its benefits reach fire-prone regions worldwide. For now, three satellites mark the start of what Earth Fire Alliance hopes becomes a global, persistent eye on wildfire . As more FireSat satellites join orbit over the coming years, the gap between a fire’s first spark and the moment responders learn about it should keep shrinking. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Who Gets to Protect the Ocean? Coral Catch is Expanding the Circle of Marine Conservation Reading Time: 3 minutes In Indonesia, Coral Catch is helping women gain the skills, confidence, and opportunities to become divers, researchers, educators, and leaders in marine conservation. Marine conservation is often measured in numbers: corals planted, reef area restored, biodiversity returning. Those numbers matter, and Coral Catch tracks them closely. But as the Indonesian nonprofit’s work grew, so did a different question: who gets the opportunity to protect these ecosystems? Coral Catch began in Indonesia’s Gili Matra Marine Protected Area with a focus on coral restoration. Over time, the team saw that its impact was reaching beyond the restoration sites. Women were growing more confident underwater, pursuing roles in marine conservation and research that once felt out of reach, and finding opportunities to become educators, advocates, and mentors. As more women moved through the program, these individual experiences began to form something larger: a pathway into marine conservation that connects training and diving opportunities with research, restoration, community engagement, and professional development. Coral Catch began to see that its impact was not only about how much reef it could restore, but also about who had the opportunity to become an ocean protector and what could happen when that opportunity continued beyond the initial training. Tania’s experience is one example of what that pathway can make possible. She grew up in Tangerang, a city far from the ocean, and arrived on Gili Air in January 2025 determined to become a marine researcher. Over nine weeks, she trained as a diver and graduated as a scientific diver, gaining not only technical skills but also the confidence to pursue a place in marine conservation. Today, Tania leads shark research in the Gili Matra Marine Protected Area, studying how tourism affects white-tip reef sharks using underwater cameras and acoustic monitoring. She has secured her own research grant and now mentors new Coral Catch participants, becoming part of the same network that helped her move forward. Cenna’s experience reflects another side of the access challenge. Growing up in Surabaya, she saw diving as something women around her did not commonly pursue. At university, she joined a diving club and loved being underwater, but field positions often required experience she had not yet had the opportunity to gain. In 2022, an online talk by a Coral Catch alumna showed Cenna that marine conservation could be a path for her too. She joined Coral Catch’s second group of participants and later worked in sustainable fisheries and community development. Today, she is Coral Catch’s Project and Partnerships Manager, supporting the program and the women coming through it. A Coral Catch Superwoman shares marine conservation lessons with local schoolchildren, extending the program’s reach far beyond the reef. Photo courtesy of Coral Catch Their journeys are now part of a much larger network. Coral Catch has trained 44 Indonesian women, with around 50% progressing to professional-level diving qualifications, and the organization aims to reach 100 women by 2030. Many alumni continue working in marine conservation or sustainable tourism, sharing what they know with their communities, returning to Coral Catch as mentors or taking on new roles, and becoming examples for younger women who may not have previously seen themselves in conservation. This network is central to how Coral Catch approaches conservation. Through its Academy and other programs, participants can move from learning and hands-on training into research, restoration, community engagement, and professional opportunities. The goal is not simply to provide access to the ocean, but to create pathways that allow people to build skills and continue contributing long after their initial training. That approach matters because access to marine conservation is not equal. Through its work, Coral Catch has seen women face barriers to marine education, diving, field experience, and conservation careers. At the same time, coral reefs support livelihoods, food security, tourism, and coastal protection, making the health of these ecosystems closely connected to the communities around them. Coral Catch’s work therefore extends beyond its training programs. The Gili Dive Club gives local community members access to diving and marine conservation training every Sunday, creating another entry point for people who want to develop practical skills and become involved in protecting their local marine environment. Coral Catch also organizes conservation expeditions twice a year, giving participants opportunities to turn travel into meaningful, hands-on experiences in marine conservation. The same approach is now being explored beyond Indonesia. Through its collaboration with Universiti Malaysia Terengganu, Coral Catch is looking at how lessons and approaches developed through its work in Indonesia can be adapted to support women and coastal communities in a different regional context. That does not mean simply copying the Indonesian model. Malaysia has its own cultural, ecological, and institutional context, so Coral Catch is working with local partners and listening to what communities and women there need. What carries forward is the broader foundation of conservation, empowerment, local capacity building, and community ownership. For Coral Catch, restoring reefs remains essential. But conservation is also about creating the people and pathways needed to sustain that work. When women have access to training, field experience, research, mentorship, and professional opportunities, they can become not just participants in conservation, but divers, researchers, educators, mentors, and leaders shaping the future of the world’s oceans. items.descriptionOriginal: “It’s only my stomach. My arms and legs are thin.” But that ‘only’ may be exactly why we need to look more closely. Some fat sits just under the skin, the kind you can pinch. But some build up deeper inside the abdomen, around the organs. That is visceral fat, and it is more closely associated with insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk. Thin arms and legs tell us what your limbs look like, not where your body is storing fat. And less muscle can matter too, because muscle is one of the main places the body uses glucose after a meal. So don’t rely only on the mirror or the weighing scale. Measure your waist. Does that number mean you definitely have a health problem? No. A tape measure cannot diagnose visceral fat. Your waist is a signal, not a verdict. If it keeps growing, keep up balanced meals, aerobic and strength activity and consistent sleep, and take the repeated trend to a qualified doctor to understand the bigger picture. That is legitimate medical guidance, not your body being judged. Talk to a qualified doctor about your metabolic health. items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στην εβδομαδιαία μας ματιά στα παρασκήνια για το τι κάνει να μιλάει η ομάδα μας. Στην τσάντα Μια παρέμβαση χαμηλού κόστους και χαμηλής τεχνολογίας σώζει ζωές σε μαιευτήρια σε όλη την Αφρική. Όπως αναφέρουν οι New York Times σε μια ιστορία που μοιράστηκε το Contributing…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. In the bag A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. “The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” Michaela says: I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. Bird’s-eye view In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds. Becca says: I kinda love these “googly-eyed buoys,” despite their uncanny resemblance to Clippy the paperclip . What else we’re reading The fix for America’s terrible internet is hiding in Tennessee — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Vox What If a Crisis Pregnancy Center Was Pro-Choice? — shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby from The Cut The planet’s vital signs are getting worse. One of the easiest fixes is your diet. — shared by Michaela Haas from Grist In other news… Just after last week’s historic midterm elections, we wrapped up The Depolarization Series , an exploration of the many ways people are defying division and really listening to those who disagree with them. You can check out the full series here — and don’t miss the many fantastic videos we shared on Instagram. The post What We’re Reading: An 80-Cent Plastic Bag Is Saving Mothers’ Lives appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Σκέφτηκαν να γράψουν τα ονόματα των επισκεπτών τους και χαιρετούσαν τον καθένα ονομαστικά την επόμενη φορά. Με την πάροδο του χρόνου, παρείχαν επιπλέον καρέκλες και κάλεσαν τους ανθρώπους να καθίσουν και να συνομιλήσουν, και ένα διαφορετικό είδος κήπου εμφανίστηκε. «Όταν πήγαμε για το δικό μας…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Fargo, North Dakota, Prakash Mathew and his wife Jane had a beautiful garden people would often stop to admire. They made a point of writing down their visitors' names and would greet each by name the next time. Over time, they provided extra chairs and invited people to sit and chat, and a different kind of garden emerged. "When we went for our walks, we could hardly walk two blocks without stopping and talking to someone." Jane died suddenly in December of last year. When summer came, Prakash continued to go to the driveway, and people still joined him. He asked, "What if we did this — sat in my driveway, but intentionally, every other week, with a topic?" Everybody loved it. Driveway Dialogues was born. A neighborhood spirit had been planted, "with a garden, a few extra chairs in front of the house, and a curiosity to care for others."

Ηλεκτρικά σχολικά λεωφορεία μεταφέρουν τώρα μαθητές στο Μπρούκλιν και το Κουίνς. First Student και Con Edison, το τοπικό βοηθητικό πρόγραμμα, fin…
items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Electric School Buses are Cutting Charging Costs in New York City Reading Time: 3 minutes Electric school buses now serve New York City students, and a trenchless charging method cut construction costs by 13%. Electric school buses now carry students across Brooklyn and Queens. First Student and Con Edison, the local utility, finished the first phase of this project . It serves the New York City Department of Education. The charging setup is what sets this project apart. First Student built its First Charge system without traditional underground trenching. That choice cut infrastructure construction costs by 13%. Trenching means digging long ditches to bury cables. That work takes time and disrupts daily life in a crowded city. Skipping it simplifies construction and helps buses reach students sooner. Here is a simple way to picture it. For every $100 a traditional installation would cost, the project saved about $13. Those savings help a fleet that needs many chargers for its electric school buses. First Charge is an above-ground system designed by bus operators, for bus operators. It is modular, meaning its parts fit together, and it can grow with a fleet. Con Edison adds that crews did not need to bury the service line to the chargers. A service line is the cable that brings power to a site. The utility says other fleet owners can copy this idea to save money and finish projects faster. Vicki Kuo, a Con Edison senior vice president, says the utility wants electric vehicles to be affordable. Lower upfront costs help make that goal real. Outside funding also helped. Con Edison and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) contributed money to the project. That included six bus vouchers and funding for four retrofit buses, which are existing buses converted to electric power. First Student also helps school districts find funding for electric school buses. Since 2023, it has secured millions of dollars in Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) funding for customers. The buses also charge on a schedule that saves money. Load management software sets charging for off-peak hours. Those are times when fewer people use power and energy costs less. The project also includes bi-directional charging technology. This allows electricity to flow both into and out of a battery. Partners are also exploring more ways to lower energy costs for fleets. Electric school buses in this project use bi-directional charging technology that lets electricity flow both into and out of a battery, while partners explore more ways to lower energy costs for fleets. Photo courtesy of First Student . Kevin Matthews, head of electrification at First Student, says scaling up electric school buses takes more than vehicles. Fleets also need the right chargers, technology, and a strong utility partner. Costs vary by district. First Student says Type C and Type D electric school buses cost around $375,000 each. Its analysis shows lifetime ownership costs matching diesel buses by 2029. Cold weather affects electric school bus range. First Student’s Quebec buses travel 80 to 90 miles per charge, or about 70 in deep cold. Newer, larger batteries reach 100 to 120 miles. Maintenance may get easier too. First Student sees fewer fluids to manage and far fewer brake problems. Fewer moving parts also cut repair time. Electric school buses offer a healthier, quieter ride. Con Edison notes the new buses produce no tailpipe emissions, which means no exhaust from the vehicle itself. They replace less efficient buses that burn fossil fuels. During the 2025-26 school year, First Student ran about 490 electric school buses. More than 550 more are on order. Its electric buses have driven over 11.2 million miles, about 450 trips around the Earth. First Student also runs a fleet of more than 48,000 vehicles across the U.S. and Canada. It carries millions of students each day. That reach means lessons from New York can travel far. Next up are 40 more electric school buses for the New York City Department of Education. First Student is also considering expanded solar use and a smart energy hub at its Brooklyn facilities. Transit agencies nationwide are also learning how electric buses can drive change. Cleaner buses can lower tailpipe pollution on every route. Could electric school buses roll out faster in other cities? First Student and Con Edison say the model can help other fleets overcome cost and construction hurdles. For students in Brooklyn and Queens, the payoff is a quieter ride on a cleaner bus. The post How Electric School Buses are Cutting Charging Costs in New York City appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Διαγωνισμοί Μουστακιού, Διακοσμημένες Καμήλες & Παιχνίδια Χωριού: Τι Σας Περιμένει στο Pushkar Fair 2026
items.titleOriginal: Moustache Contests, Decorated Camels & Village Games: What Awaits You at Pushkar Fair 2026
items.description: Στην περσινή έκθεση Pushkar, δύο επισκέπτες από την Αργεντινή, ο Pablo και ο Costa, κατάφεραν να δέσουν μια παραδοσιακή σάφα του Rajasthani (τουρμπάνι) σε μόλις 15 δευτερόλεπτα. Η εντυπωσιακή τους ταχύτητα τους χάρισε την πρώτη θέση σε έναν διαγωνισμό που προσκάλεσε διεθνείς τουρίστες να δοκιμάσουν τις δυνάμεις τους σε μια τοπική παράδοση. Σε άλλα μέρη της έκθεσης, 33 άνδρες διαγωνίστηκαν για να επιδείξουν τη φροντίδα τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: At last year's Pushkar Fair, two visitors from Argentina, Pablo and Costa, managed to tie a traditional Rajasthani safa (turban) in just 15 seconds. Their impressive speed earned them first place in a competition that invited international tourists to try their hand at a local tradition. Elsewhere at the fair, 33 men competed to show off their carefully groomed moustaches. Some had curled them into elaborate shapes, while others proudly displayed the length they had spent years growing. Among them was Ram Singh, who spoke of the pride and care that went into maintaining his moustache. These cheerful competitions are part of what makes Rajasthan's famous Pushkar Fair so special. For a few days every year, traditions that have been passed down through generations become something everyone can watch, celebrate and even participate in. And this November, the celebrations are returning. Scheduled from 17 to 24 November 2026 , the cultural programme at Pushkar Fair promises eight days of folk performances, camel decoration competitions, traditional games, music, crafts and celebrations around the town's famous lake. Here's what makes this annual gathering worth experiencing. Where even a moustache can win you a prize At Pushkar, some of the most entertaining competitions celebrate things closely associated with everyday life in Rajasthan. Take the moustache competition, for instance. For many Rajasthani men, a well-maintained moustache has long been associated with pride, personal style and identity. At Pushkar, that tradition gets its own stage. Participants arrive in traditional attire, displaying moustaches that have often taken years to grow and maintain. Judges consider their length, appearance and styling, while visitors gather to watch. The competition is scheduled to return on 21 November 2026, alongside a turban-tying contest for international visitors. And the fun continues beyond the stage. On 22 November, women are scheduled to participate in a matka race, which involves balancing a clay pot while racing towards the finish line. A musical chairs competition is also planned. The initiative has also involved rural women and artisans in preparing camel wool and making handcrafted products. Photograph: (Shutterstock) These activities offer visitors an opportunity to experience a playful side of Rajasthan's cultural traditions. For local participants, they are a chance to share familiar customs with people who may be discovering them for the first time. When traditional village games become the main attraction Remember playing gilli-danda or satoliya as a child? At Pushkar Fair, these traditional games are getting their own place in the celebrations. On 18 November, local residents and international visitors are scheduled to compete in games such as langdi taang (hopping on one leg), satoliya (a game involving stacked stones and a ball) and gilli-danda (played using two wooden sticks). The following day will bring kabaddi matches, tug-of-war, volleyball and other rural sporting competitions. A football match between local players and international visitors is also planned for the opening day, while a cricket match inspired by the film Lagaan is scheduled for 23 November. The appeal lies in how easily these games bring people together. A visitor who may know little about Rajasthan's traditions can join a familiar game, learn something new and share the experience with local participants . For children growing up in a world of mobile phones and online games, it is also an opportunity to watch traditional outdoor games being played and celebrated. What makes a camel the star of the show? Of course, no visit to Pushkar Fair would feel complete without seeing the camels. For generations, these animals have been an important part of Rajasthan's desert life, helping people travel and transport goods across difficult terrain. Today, their place in the fair extends to some of its most recognisable cultural events. On 18 November, the fair is scheduled to host camel decoration and camel dance competitions. Camel owners traditionally prepare their animals with colourful cloth, ornaments, bells and decorative accessories. Some use carefully patterned trimming to create designs in the camel's coat. The result is a display that brings together animal care, local craftsmanship and traditions associated with Rajasthan's desert communities. Behind these decorated camels are people whose knowledge of raising and caring for the animals has been passed down over generations. Among them are the Raika, also known as Rebari, a pastoral community closely associated with camel herding in western Rajasthan. Camel owners traditionally prepare their animals with colourful cloth, ornaments, bells and decorative accessories. Photograph: (Shutterstock) Their expertise includes understanding camel behaviour, caring for animals and finding suitable grazing areas across changing seasons. That knowledge remains valuable, even as camel-rearing livelihoods face growing difficulties. The fair offers visitors a glimpse of this relationship between people and animals, and an opportunity to appreciate the communities who have helped preserve it. Meet the artists keeping Rajasthan's traditions alive There is another side to Pushkar that deserves equal attention: the musicians, dancers and craftspeople who bring the celebrations to life. This year's programme begins on 17 November with group dances by schoolgirls and a mandana competition. Mandana is a traditional form of decorative art in Rajasthan, created using geometric and nature-inspired patterns, often on floors and walls. Giving this art a place at the fair helps introduce visitors to a tradition they might otherwise encounter only in homes and villages. The evenings will bring performances by local artists, including the programme Voice of Pushkar , alongside Rajasthani folk music and dance. These performances give local talent an audience that extends beyond the region. For visitors, they offer an opportunity to experience Rajasthan's cultural heritage through the people who practise these art forms. And for the performers, every appearance is another chance to introduce their work to a new audience. From handmade crafts to camel-dung notebooks Some of the most interesting stories at Pushkar Fair can also be found among the people making and selling traditional products. On 20 November, the Food and Craft Festival is scheduled to open at Shilpgram, bringing another attraction to the celebrations. Such spaces offer visitors opportunities to explore local crafts, meet artisans and discover products that reflect Rajasthan's skills and traditions. One interesting example from previous editions is Camel Charisma, a social enterprise connected to Lokhit Pashu-Palak Sansthan (LPPS), based in Sadri in Pali district. The organisation works with camel-herding communities to create new income opportunities using materials obtained from the animals. Its products have included camel-milk soaps, woollen rugs and even handmade paper produced from camel dung. At an earlier Pushkar Fair, LPPS introduced notebooks, diaries and greeting cards made using this unusual paper. The initiative has also involved rural women and artisans in preparing camel wool and making handcrafted products. What makes these efforts meaningful is the connection between traditional knowledge and present-day livelihoods. When visitors appreciate and buy locally made products, they can help create demand for the skills and materials behind them. For communities whose traditional occupations are changing, such opportunities can make a difference. A celebration that brings an entire town together While the fairgrounds host competitions and performances , the celebrations extend into the town of Pushkar itself. Around Pushkar Lake, the evenings bring gatherings, lamps, rangoli and traditional ceremonies. The fair takes place around Kartik Purnima, an important occasion for pilgrims who visit the town and its sacred lake. This year, Kartik Purnima falls on 24 November, the final day of the main cultural programme. For visitors, this offers another way to experience Pushkar: through its bustling streets, markets, cultural gatherings and the communities who return each year. The fair brings together people with different reasons for being there, from local performers and artisans to pilgrims and travellers exploring Rajasthan. And perhaps that is its greatest appeal. A visitor might arrive hoping to photograph decorated camels, then find themselves watching a traditional game, listening to a folk musician or admiring something made by a local craftsperson. Behind each experience is someone who has learnt, practised or passed down a tradition. As Pushkar Fair prepares to return this November, these are the people who make it memorable. And the most meaningful part of visiting may be the opportunity to appreciate their work, learn something from them and help ensure that Rajasthan's living traditions continue to find new audiences. Sources: 'Camels are vanishing from India's desert regions. Can a new policy push save them?' : By Sanjana Nair & Aniruddh Sheth, Published on 3 November 2025 'Explained: At Pushkar fair, renewed concern over Rajasthan's 2015 camel law' : By Deep Mukherjee, Published on 18 November 2021

Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

items.descriptionOriginal: The year I turned 30, I moved to a peaceful neighborhood on Los Angeles’ Westside. I was 10 minutes from Venice Beach and had an apartment all to myself. The only catch (besides street parking)? It was 450 square feet. A couple of friends helped me optimize the place: We assembled a custom Murphy bed, installed a wall-mounted folding table, and chose decor that made it feel joyful and airy. Though I lamented not having more space at times, I discovered that my scaled-down quarters came with some perks. Styling the studio so intentionally felt empowering, and because it was so small, I often enjoyed my meals out in the courtyard under the sun. Years later, despite having married and moved into a comfortable condo, I still occasionally yearn for more square footage, particularly during dinner parties or when family visits for the holidays. To refresh my perspective, I spoke to interior design experts and therapists who helped illuminate some of the unexpected benefits of having a smaller home — and offered tips for making the most of yours. Benefits domin_domin—iStock/Getty Images Plus Cost and Cleaning We’ll start with perhaps the most obvious but still occasionally overlooked perks: “Less square footage means less time cleaning and organizing. Owning less means spending less time managing and maintaining your belongings,” Phoenix-based interior designer Mackenzie Collier explained in an email to Nice News. “That frees up more time for hobbies, socializing, and anything else you’d rather be doing!” She added that smaller spaces force us to be more thoughtful about what we buy and why (a welcome mindset shift for many), and that the money we save on quantity can be used to invest in quality — e.g., well-built furniture, bespoke decor, art. And it’s not just our shopping carts that feel the difference, Sierra Troitsky , an interior designer in Indianapolis, pointed out. “Smaller spaces are often more economical and environmentally friendly as they cost less to heat and cool,” she said. Mental Well-Being Less square footage can contribute to a greater sense of well-being because it can encourage us to be neat and organized, “which is calming for the brain,” said Sipora Weissman , a licensed therapist in Ventura, California. In a tiny room, a pile of unfolded laundry is a lot more noticeable than in a large one, for example, so we may be more inclined to actually, you know, put it away . “As a therapist who works with adults who get overstimulated easily, living in a small space can be overwhelming or it can actually be very supportive to someone’s nervous system,” Weissman explained. “If you fill that small space with tchotchkes and clutter, that will be a recipe for an unsettled brain. There are many scientific studies that show the negative impacts of clutter on the brain. But if you take this small space living situation as an opportunity, it can be very conducive to your mental health.” More Intentional Decor Just as I experienced when decorating my tiny quarters, less to work with can have a focusing effect. “A small living room lends itself to intentional decorating because you’re forced to narrow in on fewer, impactful pieces that set the tone for the space — say, a beautiful sofa, a well-sized rug, task and accent lighting, and some meaningful artwork,” said Elena Navarro, an interior designer and professional organizer at Sparkly Maid Austin . View this post on Instagram She added: “I love that limited square footage forces you to really think through everything that you bring in the door, from new dishes to cozy throw blankets to holiday decor. Where is the item going to live? Do you use it enough to warrant giving it a permanent home?” Better for Gathering and Bonding The reason celebrity chef Ina Garten considers six people the ideal number for a dinner party is the same reason your modest home might lend itself to more meaningful gatherings: intimacy. “Small group events tend to produce an environment that allows for more personalized conversation,” explained Whitney Willborn , a Texas-based licensed clinical social worker, adding that it’s easier to not only include everyone in the conversation but also to spot when others appear to be excluded. If guests are spread out in different rooms or fragmented into groups, it’s trickier to notice when a new friend is standing awkwardly by themself, for example. Your own family might benefit from a smaller floor plan, too. Collier recently moved out of a 900-square-foot home, and her household has experienced some nostalgia for the cozier living situation. “There was nowhere to escape to, so we’d sit together, watch a movie, or play games,” she said. “Those shared moments became some of our favorite memories.” Spend More Time in Community My al fresco dining habit of yore highlights how the wide world can beckon when your indoors isn’t vast. Collier had the same experience. “I’ve found that living in a small space encourages me to spend more time outdoors and in my community,” she shared. “Whether it was tending to my garden, or heading to a local coffee shop to work, living small naturally pushed me to get out into the community more.” Tips Double Duty Interior designer Preeti Shah made her name in New York, where minuscule apartments are no big deal (one of the tiniest is an infinitesimal 55 square feet !). When she moved to an area of Houston filled with massive homes, she was bemused. At around 3,000 square feet, her house is among the smallest — yet she said it’s where her neighborhood pals prefer to hang out. Courtesy of Preeti Shah Shah’s lounge area with convertible coffee-to-dining room table A design principle Shah prioritizes, in any sized space, is double duty. “Anything I purchase, I would like for my client to be able to use it in more than just one way,” she shared. Ottomans are great for seating and storage, twin beds can become kings when guests stay over, and dining chairs should be comfy enough to be used as additional living room seating. In her own house, rather than a dining room table that sits unused, she opted for a convertible coffee table that lifts and extends to seat 10. Size and Amount Matter Troitsky explained that getting furniture that’s sized correctly can help a lot with how large your home feels (e.g., an enormous couch in a tiny bedroom might make the space seem small). But that doesn’t mean you should automatically purchase miniature versions of everything you’d buy for a bigger area. “It’s best to take inventory of what you actually use, need, and love, and start there,” Navarro said. She added: “For holiday decor, instead of trying to deck out every inch of your small living space, pick one or two areas to really lean into — the Christmas tree, the mantel, the coffee table, etc.” Get Comfortable With Borrowing Why use up valuable storage space on extra glassware and guest seating for your one annual holiday get-together when you can call a friend and ask to borrow theirs? As a bonus, it gives you both an excuse for a visit. Another option is to rent what you need when you need it. Ultimately, do your best to remember that, as Navarro put it, “the goal is always to make your guests feel at home — not to impress them with how big your place is!” RELATED: Make Your Home Happier With These Dopamine-Inducing Decorating Tips

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. In March 2020, COVID lockdowns shuttered schools around the world, including at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, where Prince Bashangezi was completing his A-Level studies. The camp sits near the Mozambique border, home to more than 17,000 people displaced by conflict across central and eastern Africa. Formal schooling stopped. Prince and a group of fellow A-Level students at USAP Community School, a school serving refugee youth in the camp, decided not to wait for it to resume. They founded TWEENS : Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. The model was built around what they had: each other. Teaching from inside the camp TWEENS began as a service learning project, with refugee students tutoring younger students in the same camp. The premise was direct. These were students who understood exactly what it meant to study without resources, without stability , often without continuous access to teachers, and in many cases without families to support them. They knew the particular difficulty of trying to build a future from inside a displaced population. So they taught each other. The program was supported by Education Matters Africa , a Zimbabwe-based nonprofit, and launched at a moment when any alternative to organized education was better than none. What began during a global lockdown became something that outlasted it. Prince was also a Waterford Kamhlaba UWC of Southern Africa alumnus, a school known for selecting students across conflict zones and economic hardship who show unusual potential and commitment. That network eventually connected him to the Global Student Haven Initiative at Pomona College in California, where he now studies computer science and economics. Marianne Langridge, who nominated Prince for this series, wrote that he “has turned his personal tragedy of losing his family during war into loving service for others.” That framing, loss converted into something that benefits others, runs through how Prince has talked about his work and what TWEENS is for. Langridge described his commitment as rooted in wanting students in refugee camps to “gain access to education so they can have hope for a better future.” Why peer tutoring works here There is something specific about a peer model in a refugee context that a standard school or aid program can’t replicate. The tutors in TWEENS are not professionals, not volunteers flying in from outside, not people working from a comfortable distance. They are students who live where the students they’re teaching live. They went through the same disruptions. Their credibility comes from proximity, not credentials. This is similar in structure to the peer-learning model that makes other youth-run programs effective, but in a refugee camp the stakes of educational continuity are different. A child who falls significantly behind in a displacement context faces a compounding disadvantage. Keeping any educational thread alive, even an informal one built by A-Level students during a lockdown, matters more than it might in a setting with backup resources. TWEENS was built on that understanding. From Tongogara to Pomona Prince arrived at Pomona College through the Global Student Haven Initiative , which supports students from refugee and displaced communities. He is studying computer science and economics, a combination that maps directly to the problems TWEENS is trying to solve: how technology and resource allocation interact to either expand or cut off access to education. Pomona profiled him in 2024 as part of a piece on Global Haven students finding opportunity in higher education. A fundraising campaign on GlobalGiving continues to support TWEENS’ operations, keeping the peer tutoring program funded as he completes his degree. What Prince Bashangezi and his fellow students built during a lockdown in a refugee camp, with nothing but time and knowledge and the willingness to share both, is still running more than five years later. TWEENS now offers an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside its original peer tutoring. To support TWEENS, visit their GlobalGiving fundraising page . The post Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .
