Διαφορετικοί πολιτισμοί σε όλο τον κόσμο έχουν αναπτύξει εδώ και καιρό μοναδικές τεχνικές για την προώθηση της υγείας, της ευτυχίας και γενικότερα…
items.descriptionOriginal: The word “wellness” may conjure images of lavish spa treatments and high-end retreats, but you don’t have to book a luxury getaway to increase your vitality — everyday activities and small, intentional habits can be equally restorative. Different cultures around the world have long developed unique techniques to promote health, happiness, and overall well-being, from the Turkish concept of savoring idle pleasure to “forest bathing” in Japan. Join us as we explore 10 wellness traditions you can adopt to infuse more peace and balance into our often-overwhelming world. 1. Schemeren | The Netherlands antolikjan/iStock If you struggle to unwind after a long day, the Dutch concept of “dusking,” or “schemeren,” may be just what you’re looking for. The practice is remarkably effortless: Simply pull up a chair and pause for a while to watch the day turn into night. “Noticing twilight requires a persistent kind of attention. It’s like a shy, rare animal. You have to take your time. Stay focused,” author Marjolijn van Heemstra told the BBC , adding that it’s an important opportunity to reconnect with the world around us. “If you don’t know a tree, even if it’s in front of your house, because you never take the time to look at it, you don’t mind it being cut,” she said. “So, it’s about seeing things and trying to establish a relationship with them and then maybe caring for them.” 2. La Passeggiata | Italy Another evening ritual — la passeggiata — is a bit more active. In Italy, many people take an after-dinner stroll around town, which offers a way to connect with neighbors, reduce stress, and improve digestion, per the BBC . Although walking is widely recommended as an accessible and effective exercise , la passeggiata is more about relaxation and social bonds than fitness. 3. Hygge | Denmark Liudmila Chernetska/iStock Scandinavian winters tend to be long and dark, but the Danish tradition of hygge can make the season more enjoyable. Stemming from an Old Norse word meaning “protected from the outside world,” hygge centers on creating a cozy, comfortable environment, with an emphasis on self-care, relaxation, and spending time with loved ones. While it’s often associated with tangible things like warm drinks and soft blankets, it’s also a mindset focused on making small moments feel more meaningful. 4. Ubuntu | Southern Africa In certain sub-Saharan African cultures, including the Zulu and Xhosa, the philosophy and practice of ubuntu emphasize the importance of community and interconnectedness. Although it goes by many different names, ubuntu is apparent throughout societies across the continent, according to The Open University . At its core, it emphasizes the role individuals play in contributing to the greater good through intentional connection, mutual support, and a shared commitment to equality, equity, and fairness. In daily life, this can look like sharing resources and checking in on neighbors. As a whole, it’s about recognizing the humanity in everyone you meet. And the benefits may extend beyond your community: Research suggests that being kind to others can help your own well-being, too. 5. Sobremesa | Spain and Latin America JulieanneBirch/iStock Another custom grounded in community is “sobremesa,” which means “upon the table.” Popular in Spain and throughout Latin America, the centuries-old way of life involves lingering after a meal to relax, savor the moment, and chat — sometimes for hours. “It’s about an interchange of experiences, knowledge, and laughs. It encourages you to be present, not worrying about your troubles, and appreciate the simple moments in life,” Mexico City restaurateur Lorea Olavarri told Food & Wine . 6. Keyif | Turkey Turkey is famous for its hammam spas, but one of its perhaps lesser-known wellness traditions can be embraced anywhere. Keyif, “an ancient art of meaningful idleness,” is a state of mind focused on finding quiet joy in simple pleasures, per Eastern Turkey Tours . Unlike simply unwinding, keyif involves being fully present and savoring the more subdued moments, from sipping your first cup of coffee in the morning while watching the sun rise to gazing out the window and listening to the birds. 7. Dadirri | Australia Thurtell/iStock In Australia’s First Nations communities, the art of deep, intentional listening — often called dadirri — is an integral part of cultural preservation, community cohesion, and individual well-being. The ancient practice encourages people to connect with one another and the natural world, according to Aboriginal learning platform Creative Spirits . But it also extends beyond that to encompass self-reflection, contemplation, and an awareness of your origins, purpose, and place in the world. “It does wonders for a person to just be still and listen to someone else talk about their life and how they probably came through things,” late Aboriginal singer-songwriter Archie Roach once said about the importance of mindful listening, per the platform, adding: “You never know what you’ll learn.” 8. Shinrin-Yoku | Japan Ample research points to the mental and physical benefits of spending time in nature, and the Japanese tradition of shinrin-yoku, or forest bathing, can help you reap them. Despite the name, there are no bathtubs involved, and even the forest is optional. All it takes is spending some time in a green space and using your senses to take it all in, whether at a botanical garden, city park, or lush woodland. Touch the soft moss, breathe in the fresh air, and listen to the birds as you gaze at the trees. “Forest therapy [can help us] see the truth that we are interconnected and interdependent. It offers us intentional time to be with ourselves, each other, and the natural world,” Regan Stacey, founder of The Forest Therapy School , told Vogue . 9. Friluftsliv | Norway Glenn Pettersen/iStock Meaning “open-air living,” this philosophy focuses on connecting with nature year-round, regardless of the weather. Popularized in the 1850s by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, friluftsliv remains a cultural mainstay throughout Scandinavia, according to the BBC . In fact, many employers in the region build outdoor recreation time into the workday. Although a Monday morning hike may not be realistic for everyone, we can all embrace friluftsliv by setting aside time to venture outside as often as we can. 10. Rhythmic Movement and Dance | Various African Cultures While not a singular tradition, dance is central to numerous cultures across the African continent and its diasporas . Although often ritualistic or ceremonial, moving one’s body rhythmically to music is also an integral part of everyday life that can foster both community and individual well-being. “Dancing is a full-body workout that benefits both the mind and body,” Liza Osagie-Clouard, orthopedic surgeon and founder of Solice Health in London, England, told British Vogue . “It improves cardiovascular health, increases flexibility, strengthens muscles, and enhances coordination,” she added. Moreover, listening to music — including the rhythmic drumming that often accompanies traditional dances — can stimulate the release of chemicals like dopamine and serotonin in the brain, helping to alleviate anxiety, enhance mood, and facilitate emotional release. items.descriptionOriginal: A Polish monk began each day with seven bows -- a gesture of apology toward a father he couldn't face. Bhikshu Jin Wei's story is not a tidy arc of spiritual progress; it's an honest account of how the hunger for transformation can become its own trap, and the gentle process of attuning to each moment. The turning came quietly, through a single word: a Thai Forest monk suggested a one-word loving-kindness mantra, and Jin Wei sat in the meditation hall asking himself what his word was. Immediately, it came: "safe". What followed was the discovery that the compassion he had been excavating through discipline had been waiting in his body all along -- "our body remembers our trauma," he reflects, "but the body also keeps the love." While on a trip back to Poland earlier this year, he experienced profound, full-circle moments along a softening journey: giving a talk at his own university and sitting down to a vegetarian lunch lovingly offered by his meat-eating family. The monastery, he suggests, is not only a physical place but a quality of listening, available to anyone willing to stop and ask what word is waiting to open their heart.

items.descriptionOriginal: Visitors to London’s British Museum can admire a remarkable example of Roman ingenuity that’s considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world. Dated to the fourth century, the ornate Lycurgus Cup is a soft jade green — or a striking ruby red, depending on where the light source is positioned. The goblet’s color-changing capability has long perplexed scientists. No one is sure exactly how it was created, but the consensus is that Romans added tiny bits of gold and silver to their glass mixture, forming layers of nanoparticles that interact with light differently depending on their size and shape. Experts had struggled to devise a reliable method of re-creating the material in quantity, but now, for the first time, the mystery appears to have been solved. Melding an ancient recipe with modern science, a glass specialist from the University of Sheffield has reproduced the effect, and commissioned a sculpture that pays homage to the original. Lisa Hollands, with the institution’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, took on the challenge, which was “very much a labor of love,” per a news release from the university. She worked with a Roman glass expert to develop a base that mimicked those used nearly two millennia ago, then set about experimenting with different furnace types, oxygen levels, and more. She said she knew it would be a much more complicated task than simply sprinkling some gold and silver nanoparticles into a mixture, but did think at one point, “If the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’” Finally, Hollands landed on a recipe for glass that looked opaque green under reflected light but red when a light was shone directly on it. “To me, it’s magic,” she told The Guardian . So how exactly does it work? “White light is made up of many different colors and you see this when there is a rainbow in the sky. Nanoparticles are much smaller than the wavelengths of light and in certain conditions they block certain colors due to the light affecting the electrons in the atoms,” she explained to the outlet. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through. If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see,” she continued. Hollands and her project manager approached U.K. glass artist Elliot Walker, who won Season 2 of Netflix’s Blown Away , to create a finished piece that could be exhibited at Sheffield’s upcoming Festival of the Mind, which runs Nov. 6-15. It will then go on permanent display at the university’s Turner Museum of Glass . “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands,” Walker said in the release. The Lycurgus Cup depicts the legend of King Lycurgus from Homer’s Iliad , showing the triumph of the Greek god Dionysus over the lawgiver Lycurgus . The 2026 homage bridges the time between the Roman artwork and now. “I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass ,” said Walker. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture , with the globe replaced by a cup.” RELATED: Researchers Re-Create 5,000-Year-Old Egyptian Blue, the World’s Oldest Synthetic Pigment Once Lost to Science

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How to Get Your Riverside, Alabama Home Ready for Summer Heat Reading Time: 6 minutes How to Get Your Riverside, Alabama Home Ready for Summer Heat Key Takeaways Simple preseason checks can uncover cooling problems before hotter weather arrives in Riverside. Clean filters, clear vents, and an unobstructed outdoor unit support steady airflow and comfort. Homeowners can handle basic upkeep, but electrical, refrigerant, and internal equipment repairs are best left to trained technicians. A heatwave backup plan helps protect people, pets, and essential supplies if cooling or power is lost. Summer heat can quickly make a Riverside, Alabama, home feel uncomfortable when an air conditioner is not ready for longer daily run times. Preparing early gives you time to identify basic airflow issues, clear outdoor equipment, and arrange an expert AC tune up Riverside homeowners may need before demand for service increases. The goal is not to disassemble your HVAC system. Instead, focus on safe, visible maintenance tasks that help your home retain cooled air and reveal signs that deserve professional attention. Taking notes as you inspect the system can also be useful. Record unusual sounds, odors, water, uneven room temperatures, or thermostat behavior so you can describe the issue clearly if service is needed later. Why Summer Preparation Matters When temperatures rise, an air conditioner must remove heat from indoors for longer periods. A clogged filter, a blocked return grille, a drainage issue, or a struggling component may be less noticeable in mild weather but become much more apparent during the first sustained hot spell. Preparing before peak heat also reduces the chance that a small concern becomes an urgent comfort problem. Riverside households can also review the practical safety guidance in the EPA’s information on extreme heat as they make their summer plans. Preparation also makes it easier to distinguish between a minor comfort issue and a problem that requires prompt attention. For example, a room that has always received intense afternoon sun may need better shading. In contrast, a room that suddenly has low airflow could indicate an obstructed vent, a filter issue, or equipment failure. Addressing visible issues early can help avoid unnecessary stress during high outdoor temperatures. The Homeowner Cooling Checklist Set aside a short amount of time to walk through this list before summer settles in: Inspect or replace the air filter. Move furniture, rugs, and curtains away from supply vents and return grilles. Remove leaves, grass clippings, and loose debris around the outdoor unit. Test the thermostat in cooling mode. Look for water near the indoor equipment. Listen for unusual sounds when the system starts. Schedule service if you find warning signs. As you complete the checklist, avoid making multiple adjustments at once. Change or inspect the filter, confirm that vents are open, and then allow the system time to operate normally. This approach makes it easier to notice whether a particular step improved comfort or whether the concern remains. Keep access paths to both indoor and outdoor equipment clear so a technician can inspect the system safely if an appointment becomes necessary. Check Filters and Airflow A dirty filter restricts airflow, which can reduce cooling effectiveness and place additional strain on the system. Use the filter size and type specified for your equipment, and inspect it regularly. Homes with pets, ongoing renovations, heavy dust, or household members with allergy concerns may need more frequent checks. Keep supply vents open, and ensure that sofas, bookcases, curtains, or storage bins do not cover the return grilles. A filter should capture airborne particles without being so restrictive that it reduces the airflow your system needs. When checking a filter, make sure it is installed in the correct direction. Many filters include an arrow that should point toward the equipment and in the direction of airflow. Also, look at the filter rack or access door after replacing it; a poorly seated filter can leave gaps that allow unfiltered air and dust to bypass the filter. Clear the Outdoor Unit The outdoor portion of a central air-conditioning system releases heat collected from inside the house. Keep the area around it free of weeds, leaves, grass clippings, and stacked items so air can move around the cabinet. Trim back vegetation that crowds the unit, while avoiding aggressive cutting or contact with the equipment. After mowing or yard work, take a quick look at the area around the unit. Grass clippings and loose debris can collect against the cabinet or around the base. Avoid placing lawn tools, trash containers, decorations, or storage items next to the equipment, even temporarily, because they can limit airflow and make future inspection more difficult. Do not open electrical panels, straighten thin metal fins, or spray the unit with high-pressure water. Damaged wiring, severe corrosion, bent fins, or obvious physical damage are reasons to stop and arrange a professional inspection. Test the Thermostat Set the thermostat to cooling mode. Choose a setting below the current indoor temperature. Allow several minutes for a normal startup delay. Confirm that cool air reaches the main living spaces. Replace batteries if the display is fading, blank, or unresponsive. Setting the thermostat far below your desired temperature does not make the system cool faster. It simply calls for a longer cooling cycle, which can increase energy use. If your thermostat has a schedule or programmable settings, review them before the hottest part of the season. Confirm that the programmed temperatures match the household’s routine and that vacation or away settings have not been left on accidentally. Keep the thermostat area clear of lamps, electronics, and direct sunlight when possible, as nearby heat can affect the device’s readings. Reduce Heat Inside the Home Good cooling performance depends on more than the equipment; close blinds, drapes, or shades on windows that receive strong morning or afternoon sun. Keep exterior doors closed during the hottest part of the day, and use ovens, dryers, and other heat-producing appliances during cooler hours when practical. Check for obvious gaps around doors and windows, then repair damaged weatherstripping or seals. Ceiling fans can make people feel cooler by moving air across the skin, but they do not lower the room’s actual temperature. Over the longer term, attic insulation, air sealing, and duct repairs can help limit unwanted heat gain. For best comfort, use ceiling fans only in occupied rooms and turn them off when the room is empty. If a particular room consistently feels warmer, compare it with the rest of the home at different times of day. Closing window coverings before direct sunlight enters the room, keeping doors positioned to support airflow, and avoiding heat-producing activities there can make a noticeable difference without changing the thermostat for the entire house. Know When to Call a Professional Leave refrigerant work, capacitor testing, electrical repairs, internal coil access, and major drainage repairs to a qualified HVAC professional. These tasks can involve electrical hazards, specialized tools, and components that should not be handled casually. A professional should also evaluate recurring problems rather than just the most visible symptom. For instance, repeatedly changing a filter will not correct a persistent drainage problem, an electrical fault, a damaged component, or a duct issue. If the system has a history of short-cycling, uneven cooling, or water near the equipment, note when the problem occurs and whether it has become more frequent. Warning Signs That Need Attention Warm air or weak airflow from multiple vents. Repeated breaker trips. Water is pooling near indoor equipment. Grinding, buzzing, rattling, burning, or strong musty odors. Frequent starts and stops. A noticeable, unexplained increase in energy use. What a Professional Inspection May Cover A service visit may include electrical safety checks, airflow and temperature testing, thermostat operation, condensate-drain evaluation, inspection of coils and components, and refrigerant-system testing when needed. Before the appointment, make a list of the symptoms you have noticed, including which rooms feel different and whether the issue occurs at a certain time of day. If possible, note whether the problem started suddenly or developed gradually. These details can help the technician understand the situation and focus the inspection on likely causes. Create a Heatwave Plan Choose a room that can serve as a temporary comfort space if the main system has trouble. Keep drinking water, medications, phone chargers, flashlights, and battery-powered fans accessible. Know which nearby public locations may offer air conditioning, and check on older adults, young children, people with health conditions, and pets. It is also helpful to decide in advance who will be responsible for checking on family members, neighbors, or friends who may be more vulnerable to heat. Keep important contact numbers available in case cellular devices need to be conserved. If you use medical equipment that depends on electricity, discuss backup arrangements and emergency planning needs with the appropriate health care provider or equipment supplier before severe heat arrives. During dangerous heat, portable fans may improve comfort but cannot prevent heat illness in very hot rooms. The EPA’s indoor heat safety advice also recommends using generators outdoors and at least 20 feet away from buildings, doors, windows, and vents. Common Questions When should I prepare my cooling system? Start before the first extended stretch of hot weather. Early preparation leaves more time to address a problem without waiting through a peak-season service rush. It also allows you to test the thermostat and cooling operation when the home does not yet rely on the system for all-day use. How often should I change an air filter? Follow the equipment maker’s guidance and inspect the filter regularly. Replacement timing depends on the filter type, household conditions, pets, dust, and system use. A visual inspection is often more useful than relying only on a calendar reminder, especially during periods of heavier system use. Why is one room hotter than the rest of the house? Common causes include direct sun exposure, blocked vents, dirty filters, duct leakage, inadequate insulation, and airflow or equipment problems. Start with simple checks, such as window coverings and blocked vents, then seek professional advice if the difference persists or affects several rooms. What if the AC stops during a heatwave? Check thermostat settings, batteries, the filter, and whether a breaker has tripped once. Do not keep resetting a breaker that trips again. If indoor temperatures climb, move people and pets to a cooler location and call a qualified professional. Final Steps Before Summer A few early checks can make a Riverside home more comfortable when summer heat arrives. Handle simple upkeep, keep air moving freely, reduce indoor heat gain, and seek professional help when symptoms suggest electrical, refrigerant, drainage, or mechanical trouble. Preparing your home and household plan before the hottest days arrive can make it easier to respond calmly if comfort problems occur. items.description: Περιγραφή επεισοδίου: Δύο θραύσματα κοραλλιών έπεσαν σε μια δεξαμενή εργαστηρίου του Στάνφορντ και έτυχε να αγγίξουν, και μέσα σε λίγες μέρες το λευκασμένο άρχισε να απορροφά υγιή φύκια απευθείας από το σημείο επαφής με τον γείτονά του. Οι ερευνητές δεν είχαν σχεδιάσει αυτό το πείραμα, το οποίο είναι μέρος αυτού που κάνει την ανακάλυψη τόσο εντυπωσιακή: έναν πιθανό μηχανισμό ανάκτησης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank and happened to touch, and within days the bleached one started absorbing healthy algae directly through the contact point with its neighbor. The researchers hadn’t designed that experiment, which is part of what makes the discovery so striking: a potential recovery mechanism for bleached coral hiding in plain sight, requiring nothing more than the right genetic match and direct physical contact. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including a brain therapy reporting 68 percent remission for PTSD when decades of medication have only reached 11, a wildlife sanctuary in Austin that runs on Twitch donations and reaches the conservation audience that broadcast nature documentaries never could, and the solar panels now legal for California renters that require no contractor, no roof, and no tens of thousands of dollars upfront. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Intro Arielle: Hello, it’s Arielle. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. How are you, Karissa? Karissa: Um, feeling pretty tired. Trying to adjust to the time change here, so. Arielle: Oh, yeah. You guys had your time change in the States this past weekend, right? Karissa: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and I know you had it the weekend before. But yeah, this week has been, been all about adjustment. Arielle: It’s a bit of a transition period. I feel like a lot of my friends are going through transitions right now, and it kind of aligns with the seasons. And also Thanksgiving is coming up. Well, I mean, Canadian Thanksgiving already happened in October, and that’s what I grew up with. But you guys have your Thanksgiving soon. And, uh, to celebrate, we’re doing our local changemaker series like we do every year. Karissa: Yeah, it’s always one of our favorite times of year, too, to give back to The Optimist Daily community and report on the changemakers that are making a difference in your lives and your communities. Speaking of gratitude, we’re very grateful for all of you Optimists who keep The Optimist Daily going in our shared resolve to get positive news out there. And we also wanna thank our Emissaries, who are the financial supporters of The Optimist Daily. Arielle: We have big love for our Emissaries. They help us keep the lights on here. But there are a lot of free ways that you can help support this mission as well, ’cause we know that not everybody has the budget to donate, and that’s completely fine. But if you wanted to help our cause in other ways, you can follow us on socials. We are @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism. And along with that, you can share our content on your own personal stories or send them directly to friends and family who you think need a little bit more positivity in their lives. All of that helps us out a lot. Karissa: You can also email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com, or reach out to us on any of the platforms we’re on. Arielle: All right. Well, with all of that said and done, I think I’m going to jump into this week’s solutions. Sardinian restaurants banning phones Arielle: The first one is titled “Sardinian restaurants are banning phones for families at meals”. So in Sardinia, 15 restaurants are asking families to put their phones away when they sit down to eat. In exchange, staff hand them a box of games designed by pediatricians to help parents and kids actually talk to each other. Do you find yourself either seeing people out at a restaurant who aren’t actually engaging with each other ’cause they’re on their phones, or do you find yourself doing that as well, Karissa? Karissa: I mean, I definitely see people doing it, and I try my hardest not to do it. Usually when I’m out at dinner it’s with someone maybe I haven’t seen in a while, so we have lots to talk about, so really try not to. But I, I mean, I can be guilty sometimes if I’m just out at dinner, um, with maybe my family or my boyfriend because, you know, we’re talking all the time, so I’m like, “Well, let me just pull it out for a second while we’re waiting.” Arielle: Yeah, I try my best to just keep my phone, um, where I can’t see it when I’m with other people. Yeah. But I… If I’m eating by myself then I will- Karissa: Mm. Arielle: … um, distract myself with my phone, you know? What I like about this screen time story is that it’s a little bit different from the typical one that you see. It’s not, like, just a lecture or, or, like, a rule. There’s actually a- Yeah … kit. It’s a pediatrician-designed game box that the restaurant itself will hand you so that you have something in your hands other than a phone. So that to me is, like, a structural solution and not so much of a moral one. Or it is, but, like, there’s more structure to it. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Anna Cau, she’s the Children’s Ombudsman, which is an independent official appointed to receive, investigate, and help resolve complaints made by individuals against government agencies, public authorities, or private organizations, if you didn’t know. That I got from Wikipedia. But she’s the woman who designed the scheme, and she makes this point: Most screen time debates put the whole problem on parents, and she’s saying the spaces families move through, like restaurants and anywhere in public life, they should also be part of the solution. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And this is based in Sardinia, uh, which is in Italy. And there, the communal meal carries a lot of cultural weight. Yeah. I mean, it carries weight everywhere because eating is such a social human practice. But in Italy especially, if the- Karissa: Yeah … Arielle: dinner table is losing to screens over there, then that’s a, a real signal. So yeah, I just really enjoyed reading about this solution, and maybe it will inspire other people who are listening to have their own kind of phone-free dinners. And, uh, you know, I’m sure you can look up engaging questions online or create your own questions to ask your family members as well. You don’t need to have this, uh, specific game box or pediatrician-designed kit. California balcony solar for renters Arielle: The next solution is titled “California legalizes balcony solar for renters and beyond”. We’ve been hearing a lot about solar energy and apartment dwellers being able to participate in that, but this is quite local to you, Karissa, ’cause California just legalized plug-in solar panels, and for the first time, that includes renters. Panels that cost a few hundred dollars that you hang off your balcony or stick outside a window that could cut your electricity bill by up to $500 a year are now legal. So there’s no contractor, no roof, no tens of thousands of dollars upfront for Californians who live in apartments. California is the 10th state to pass this kind of law. It’s the biggest electricity market in the country, so when California moves, then manufacturers basically have to follow. The goal advocates keep describing is plug-in solar on a shelf at a hardware store like any other appliance, and that’s finally a realistic near-term thing. First green star discovered Arielle: The next solution is a pretty fun one. It’s titled “Astronomers discovered first green star ever, and it’s powered by a dead planet’s chemistry”. Astronomers just found the first green star ever documented, a white dwarf that glows chartreuse, not because of temperature, but because it absorbed sodium from a planetary system it destroyed. A star that ate its planets and turned green. It’s like a sci-fi. I was just- Yeah … fascinated by this whole solution. We’ve always assumed star colors track with temperature, like iron heating in a blacksmith’s forge, if you can imagine, like, it goes from red to white hot, and this star kind of broke that model. Its color is a chemical record of what it’s consumed. Carbon-rich atmospheres glow pink or purple. Stars that absorbed asteroid or planetary material go yellow. But then this one went green. There’s a lot more on the science within the article itself. Uh, but yeah, I just found the whole thing quite interesting. I just think it’s really cool to think about all of this unexpected, completely surprising stuff happening in this universe. Great Koala National Park Arielle: Okay, moving on to the next solution, which is titled, “How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in New South Wales, Australia.” After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and 14 hours of parliamentary debate, Australia’s Great Koala National Park is officially real. It’s 478,000 hectares of protected habitat, which is roughly 1.2 million acres, and the thing that finally made it financially viable was carbon credits. The part about carbon credits is what makes the economics work. The government registered over 117,000 hectares of the park state forests with the Federal Clean Energy Regulator. By ending native forest logging there, they can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest generates more revenue than logged timber, it turns out, and that’s the financial argument that helped get this through. The article goes into the human cost. It didn’t wanna glaze over that detail. The forestry corporation already cut 30-plus jobs in Coffs Harbour before the park was even finalized, and then there’s also timber suppliers and trucking companies, engineering firms, all of these places of employment that have to let a lot of people go. So the government- Yeah … is committed to moving displaced workers into national parks roles, but that transition is still underway, and I’m sure it will go through some growing pains. Ashley Love, the conservationist who started this campaign after locals told him koalas weren’t as common as they used to be, called the result, “Quite fragmented with connectivity gaps still to close.” But he’s already pushing for the sections that didn’t make it into the park. And yeah, after a decade, he sounds less frustrated than just persistent, because this is still such an accomplishment. Karissa: Conservation campaigns that connect land protection to economic logic are always gonna be more viable. I think it’s a good model to follow, and, um, just a, a win for the koalas. Arielle: Mm-hmm. It’s a win for the koalas, and a win for Australia’s broader biodiversity as a whole. Coral healing through touch Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand over the reins to Karissa is “Stanford scientists discovered bleached coral can heal through touch”. Two coral fragments accidentally fell over and touched each other in a Stanford lab tank. Within days, the fragment that was bleached started recovering, absorbing healthy algae directly through the point of contact with the healthy coral fragment. The researchers were blown away because this was not supposed to happen. It was not really their experiment at all. What makes it scientifically interesting is how specific the conditions have to be for this to happen. It only works with direct physical contact and only between genetically identical corals. If you separate them by a few millimeters, then nothing will happen. If you introduce a different genetic background, then they reject each other, much like a mismatched organ transplant. Genetic twins in contact create what the team calls a tissue bridge, which is a nutrient highway between them The IUCN announced that about 96% of the world’s shallow water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, so this discovery is a glimmer of hope in a very dark picture. Maya Higa’s wildlife sanctuary on Twitch Karissa: Okay, so this is one of our local Change Makers series articles, and it’s about Maya Higa, who built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch funded by the people who watch it. Earlier this year, Maya was on a trip to Dominica and was offered the chance to swim with sperm whales, and she said no. Her followers couldn’t be there, and that one decision pretty much captures what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do and explains how a Twitch stream became a $7.5 million conservation platform. Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin and a virtual conservation classroom. Animal ambassadors, animals that can’t survive in the wild, live at the sanctuary, while a 24/7 live stream lets viewers watch, learn, and get to know individual animals by name. And Maya’s background isn’t just as a creator. She’s a former zookeeper with a falconry license and a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. So all that knowledge is what this stream runs on. The demographic she’s reaching is one that traditional conservation has struggled to reach for decades. She’s reaching 18 to 30-year-olds through social media in ways that broadcast nature documentaries never could. Arielle: Yeah, it’s such a smart move. You know, a lot of the time the depiction of the younger generation is that their attention spans are really, um, short, which in some ways is true, but there’s also a lot of young people who just love to watch streams, and those are like- Yeah … long-form, like the longest form content there is. So yeah, really big shout-out to Maya. This is an incredible project. And yeah, I, I think I’m gonna start watching … the animals as well. Karissa: I love this whole idea, and of course they’re targeting the younger viewers, but I think it kind of reaches across the ages as well. Um, my mind goes to in California, Jackie and Shadow, the bald eagles that- Yeah lived in Big Bear Lake, I think captured the hearts of many. So once again, congrats to Maya, and check out the article for more details. Solar kits for disaster relief Karissa: The next solution is “Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like”. Every morning in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo and tarpaulin shelter and puts out a solar panel. He’s done it for six years since his family fled the Rohingya crackdown in Myanmar. That one panel is how his whole family charges phones, cooks with light, and keeps fans running through the heat. And this story is about what this technology is actually for. The range of where this is happening right now is pretty striking. Doctors Without Borders is running a tuberculosis clinic on solar in Karachi, and UN water filtration on solar in South Sudan. And kits were distributed after Nepal’s floods that killed over 1,400 people. And a nonprofit in Ukraine has given kits to thousands of families, including 75 and 80-year-old grandparents who just plug them in. The CEO said, “It’s just a matter of plug and play for these solar relief kits.” And I mean, that goes back to our earlier solution of the plug-in balcony solar panels. But switching from diesel to solar is harder than it sounds for aid organizations because long-running generator contracts are still going on. There’s new distribution chains that have to be navigated in genuinely dangerous conditions. In addition, recent donor funding cuts have made it harder to transition to new technology. So one program leader said flat out, “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut.” Arielle: Yeah, it’s interesting. Whenever I think about solar panels, I think about the types of solutions that we’ve been hearing about so far, like the rooftop solar in Australia for apartments or the plug-in solar or solar panels above farm fields. But I don’t really think about it in this context where it could be so, so useful for disaster relief or- Yeah for places that don’t have access to a reliable grid. Uh, so I think it’s really encouraging that this technology is reaching all corners of the world for all types of contexts and situations. Household uses for toothpaste Karissa: The next story is a lifestyle solution, and it’s “Eight surprising household uses for toothpaste from a pro cleaner”. So there’s probably a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now, and if it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool just sitting in the drawer. A professional cleaner shared the eight household jobs she regularly uses it for, and some of them are actually not that obvious. Plain, white, non-gel toothpaste has mild abrasive particles that work like an ultra-fine sandpaper, and that’s why it can buff out light scratches on glass, phone screens, and wood surfaces, and polish metal fixtures, so lots of different uses. Gel toothpaste doesn’t have those particles, so it doesn’t work the same way, and that’s just something to keep in mind when you reach for that toothpaste. One use I was surprised to read is using toothpaste for a fogged car headlight, and it’s one that a lot of people haven’t heard, and it’s really simple. You just rub toothpaste over the lens in small circles for about a minute or two, rinse, dry, and repeat if needed. So no specialty product is required to clear up those fogged headlights. There’s just kind of this huge appetite right now, especially with the economy and the whole idea of sustainability as well, to, you know, use things you already own and get creative with them. It’s practical, it’s low cost, and it’s also satisfying as well. Brain therapy for PTSD Karissa: Moving on to the next solution, “Personalized brain therapy hits 68% remission for PTSD”. The best FDA-approved medications for PTSD have a remission rate of about 11%. But a newly FDA-cleared brain therapy just reported a 68% remission, and that’s not a typo. That is a big difference. It’s the first non-drug treatment specifically cleared for PTSD since the diagnosis was formally recognized in 1980. How this therapy works is that you get an EEG that maps your specific brain electrical activity, and an AI algorithm builds a personalized stimulation plan from that data. Then a coil placed against your scalp delivers targeted magnetic pulses, and you do this for five sessions a week for five to six weeks. The lead researcher described standard brain stimulation as covering the leak with a tarp, and this treatment tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. This is important for many different populations because about 6% of Americans will experience PTSD in their lifetime with higher rates among women and veterans. Approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day in the US. The two SSRIs approved for PTSD have been the only FDA-approved options since 1980, and 11% remission means the vast majority haven’t gotten there on medications alone. So this is a really great breakthrough, and of course, accessibility is going to be the next hurdle. Um, you know, teams are actively trying to work on getting this covered by insurance, and FDA clearance is not the same as accessibility, so this gap is the next fight Volunteering this Thanksgiving Karissa: The final solution I have to share is “The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving, 17 options for every schedule”. Every year around Thanksgiving, a lot of people have the same thought, “This is the year I actually do something.” And then they show up at a food bank and find out every other person in town had the same idea. There’s actually a smarter way to do this, and several options that don’t even require leaving your couch at all. So I think the most important point out of this article, even though it gives tips to volunteer and help around, is that holiday demand often creates more volunteers than organizations can actually use on Thanksgiving Day itself. And a lot of that is directed at food banks. So if you want your time to count, definitely call ahead and see if you’re needed. And if you get redirected because a location is at capacity, ask when they need people the most. The answer is almost always in February, when the holiday energy has faded out, but the need hasn’t. And I think that’s just a really good point. These organizations need your help year-round, and that’s important to keep in mind. So this list covers every kind of situation, whether it’s Feeding America, Meals on Wheels, and Operation Turkey, and about the tightly organized shifts they have. But it also covers options that are remote, like writing letters to deployed service members through Support Our Troops, and animal shelters for people who are better with dogs than crowds. So lots of ways to volunteer this giving, thankful, grateful season. So yeah, I think it’s just a great reminder, and hard to believe that Thanksgiving is already around the corner. Arielle: Yeah, I totally agree. I, I didn’t really think too much about the oversaturation in the volunteering space for the holiday season. It does make sense, though. So, you know, I, I think if you’re interested in volunteering and just haven’t gotten around to it yet, then maybe the holiday season is a great place to start. But then it could be your gateway into doing it- Karissa: Yeah … Arielle: more regularly as well. Outro & quote Karissa: Well, that’s all of the positive news we had to share this week on The Optimist Daily. But before we go, we’ll leave you off with a quote. ” Arielle: Having a good time together is the essence of lovingness and the best means of increasing it.” That’s from Benjamin Spock, and I think that’s a great quote to go with quite a few of our stories today. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. That’s why I wanted to include it in today’s, uh, roundup. Arielle: We will be back next week with more solutions. In the meantime, Karissa and I wish all of you Optimists and Emissaries a wonderful weekend. Karissa: Yeah. Bye, everyone. Arielle: Bye.
